video_title: 🎓 School Rules! by Robert Munsch
description:
School Rules! by Robert Munsch, illustrated by Dave Whamond. Read by Riko.

Cassandra LOVES school so much she never, ever wants to leave!

Cassandra does not want to go home from school. She stays after the nice teacher
leaves. She stays while the janitor with a tattoo mops the floors. She stays after the
slightly scary principal turns off all the lights and goes home. She plays and reads
until after dark, when her mom and dad realize she is missing and come in a panic
to take her home.

The next day, Cassandra gets up, eats breakfast, gets on her bike and heads off to
school — but it is Saturday and all the doors and windows are locked. So on her
way back home she stops by the store and places an order.

The next day she looks out the window to find her purchase has been delivered —
there is a brand-new red-brick school with a nice teacher, a slightly scary principal,
and a janitor with tattoos in her very own backyard, so she can have school any
time she likes!

video_title: My Grandma Can Do Anything in the Adirondacks #educational #toddlers #kindergarten #kidsbooks #story
description:
"My Grandma Can Do Anything in the Adirondacks" sounds like a wonderful and heartwarming children's book idea. It captures the spirit of adventure, family, and the unique beauty of the Adirondack Mountains.

Here is a potential outline, story, and themes for such a book.

Book Concept: "My Grandma Can Do Anything in the Adirondacks"
Target Age: 4-8 years old

Themes: Adventure, Family, Nature, Confidence, Intergenerational Bonding, Love for the Outdoors.

Setting: The Adirondack Mountains in upstate New York, featuring iconic elements like high peaks, serene lakes, loons, pine forests, and cozy cabins.

Story Outline & Sample Text
(The book would be filled with vibrant, warm illustrations showing a spirited, active grandma and her admiring grandchild.)

Page 1 (Opening Spread):

Illustration: A wide shot of the Adirondack mountains from a lake. The sun is rising, mist is on the water. A loon is swimming.

Text: "Every summer, I pack my backpack and go to my favorite place in the world: my grandma's house in the Adirondacks."

Page 2-3:

Illustration: Grandma, wearing well-loved hiking boots and a flannel shirt, is lacing up her boots on the porch of a rustic cabin. The child is mimicking her.

Text: "And let me tell you a secret... my grandma can do ANYTHING."

Page 4-5: (Hiking)

Illustration: Grandma and the child hiking up a rocky trail. Grandma is pointing out a interesting mushroom or a salamander on a rock.

Text: "She can climb a mountain trail, higher than the tallest pine tree, and still have breath to sing a silly song."

Page 6-7: (Canoeing)

Illustration: They are in a red canoe on a still, glassy lake. Grandma is dipping her paddle silently into the water. A loon is nearby.

Text: "She can paddle a canoe so quietly, the loons think we're just a ripple on the water."

Page 8-9: (Identifying Nature)

Illustration: Grandma is kneeling down, showing the child how to identify animal tracks (maybe deer or raccoon) in the mud.

Text: "She can read the secret stories written in the mud by raccoons and deer."

Page 10-11: (Fishing)

Illustration: Sitting on a sun-drenched dock, legs dangling in the water. Grandma is helping the child cast a fishing line.

Text: "She can cast a fishing line right to the spot where the sunfish are dreaming."

Page 12-13: (Weather Wisdom)

Illustration: Dark clouds are rolling over the mountains. Grandma is looking at the sky, smelling the air, while they quickly pack a picnic blanket.

Text: "She can smell a rainstorm coming before the first drop even falls, and find the coziest spot to wait it out."

Page 14-15: (Campfire)

Illustration: The rain is falling but they are under a lean-to. Grandma is expertly building a small campfire, sparks flying up into the darkening sky.

Text: "She can build a crackling campfire that chases away the shivers and toasts the perfect marshmallow—golden brown, never black!"

Page 16-17: (Stargazing)

Illustration: Night has fallen. The sky is clear and full of stars. Grandma and the child are wrapped in a blanket, looking up. She's pointing out constellations.

Text: "And when the sky is filled with a million stars, she can find the Big Dipper and tell me stories about the Milky Way."

Page 18-19: (The Real Magic)

Illustration: A quieter, more intimate illustration. They are back on the cabin porch, rocking in chairs, drinking hot cocoa. Grandma has her arm around the child, who is looking up at her with love and admiration.

Text: "But the very best thing my grandma can do... isn't climbing or paddling or fishing..."

Page 20-21 (Final Spread):

Illustration: A close-up of Grandma and the child hugging.

Text: "...it's making me feel brave, and smart, and like I can do anything in the Adirondacks, too."

Text (smaller, on the last page): "Just like her."

description:
Ewoks: The Battle for Endor Read Along (1985) The army of the Marauders, led by by King Terak and the witch Charal attack the Ewoks village. The parents and the brother of Cindel all die in this attack. Cindel and the Ewok Wicket escape and in a forrest they meet Teek a naughty and very fast animal. Teek takes them to a house in which a old man, Noa, lives. Like Cindel he also crashed with his Starcruiser on Endor. Together they fight Terak and Charal.

► Cast of the full movie version were...

Wilford Brimley Noa
Warwick Davis Wicket
Aubree Miller Cindel
Siân Phillips Charal

Niki Botelho Teek

Tony Cox Willy

Johnny Weissmuller Jr. Card Player #2
Matthew Roloff Ewok with Crutches

► Plot

While the Towani family (Jeremitt, Catrine, Mace, and Cindel) are preparing to leave the forest moon of Endor, the Ewok village is attacked by a group of Marauders (originally crash landed from Sanyassa) led by Terak and his witch-like sorceress Charal. Many Ewoks are killed. Cindel escapes, but is forced to leave Jeremitt, Catrine, and Mace to their doom, both parents having already been hit by enemy fire; her mother and brother killed when a Marauder blaster-cannon destroys a hut in which they had taken refuge from the battle.

While running away from the carnage, Cindel and Wicket meet Teek, a small, fast native of Endor. Teek takes them to the home of Noa Briqualon, a human man who is angered by their uninvited presence, and throws them out. Eventually he proves himself to be a kindhearted man, letting Teek steal food for them, and inviting the two in when they attempt to build a fire for warmth.

At the Marauders' castle, Charal is ordered by Terak to find Cindel, assuming she knows how to use "the power" in the energy-cell stolen from Jeremitt's star cruiser. Meanwhile, Noa, Cindel, and Wicket are becoming friends. It is revealed that Noa is rebuilding his own broken star cruiser, only missing the energy-cell.

Cindel is awakened one morning by a song her mother used to sing to her. She follows the voice to find a beautiful woman singing. The woman transforms into Charal, who takes her to Terak. He orders her to activate "the power." When she cannot, she and Charal are both imprisoned with the Ewoks. Outside, Noa, Wicket, and Teek sneak into the castle, making their way to the cellblock, where they free Cindel and the other Ewoks. They escape with the energy-cell.

Terak, Charal, and the Marauders pursue them back to the ship, where Wicket leads the Ewoks in defense of the cruiser, and Noa installs the energy-cell in his ship. The Ewoks put up a valiant effort, and are nearly beaten by the time Noa powers up the ship and uses its formidable laser cannons to fend off the Marauders. When Cindel goes to save Wicket, she is captured by Terak, even as the other Marauders retreat. Terak and Noa face off, with Wicket finally coming to the rescue, killing Terak and simultaneously leaving Charal trapped in bird form for eternity.

Shortly thereafter, goodbyes are said, as Noa and Cindel leave the forest moon of Endor aboard Noa's starship.

video_title: My WORST Best Friend Read Aloud by Reading Pioneers Academy
description:
My Worst Best Friend Bundle #1 is a compilation of the first four books in Julie Cavacco's humorous My Worst Best Friend series. These stories are great for emerging readers, but also have great appeal to readers of all levels. The series features the familiar antics and conflicts often found between good friends with different natures and highlights the rewards and challenges of childhood friendship.

Originally written for a late-reading fifth grade boy. He couldn't find a book that he was willing to read at his reading level because the books available in the library, where she was a children's librarian, were too "babyish". it has appealed to early readers, reluctant readers, school psychologists, ESL students, and adult students who never mastered a higher level of reading who are working on becoming fully literate.

They've been in classrooms as an option for silent reading periods where a student at any level can pick up the book and not feel like they are reading a "little kid's" book. Julie observed, after years of substituting at the elementary school level, that behavior and self-esteem are tied into the ability to read. She has seen success and how it can improve both behavior and self-esteem as students become stronger readers.

The cover piqued his interest, but Olly didn’t want to risk his reputation by letting his classmates see him voluntarily reading. So rather than check out the book, he stole it.

He recounts how this book — and a little nudge from two helpful librarians — turned him around academically.

This all-new animated short is presented as part of the new StoryCorps animation season, “Moments that Define,” where StoryCorps participants share the turning points that have shaped them.

video_title: ish (to embrace their creativity, trust their instincts,) Kids Picture Story Book || Read Aloud
description:
“Ish” is a delightful children’s book written and illustrated by Peter H. Reynolds. In this heartwarming tale, we meet a young artist named Ramon, who loves to draw. However, when his older brother, Leonardo, criticizes his artwork, Ramon becomes disheartened. Leonardo tells him that his drawings don’t look like real objects, and Ramon feels like he has lost his artistic spark.

But then, Ramon’s little sister, Marisol, shows him a different perspective. She admires his drawings and sees beauty in their unique qualities. Marisol introduces Ramon to the concept of “ish”—the idea that art doesn’t have to be perfect or exact. Instead, it can capture the essence of something, even if it’s not a precise representation.

Inspired by Marisol’s wisdom, Ramon begins to create again. He draws “tree-ish” and “fish-ish” pictures, embracing imperfection and celebrating the spirit of creativity. Through his journey, Ramon learns that art is about expressing feelings and ideas, rather than rigid accuracy.

“Ish” encourages young readers to embrace their creativity, trust their instincts, and find joy in the process of making art. It’s a heartwarming reminder that perfection isn’t necessary—what matters is the joy of creating something uniquely “ish.” 🎨(AI generated).

description:
Let's dive into the buzzing world of bees! This is everything you need to know, made just for kids.

What is a Bee?
Bees are amazing flying insects, and they are super important to our planet. You might think they're just for making honey, but they do a job that's even more critical!

Think of them as tiny, fuzzy superheroes of nature.

The Bee-autiful Body of a Bee
A bee's body has three main parts, just like other insects:

Head: This is where the important stuff is!

Eyes: Bees have five eyes! Two big ones on the side and three tiny ones on top of their head. This helps them see all around.

Antennae: These are like tiny feelers that help them smell and touch things.

Tongue: A long, straw-like tongue for drinking nectar from flowers.

Thorax: This is the bee's engine room!

Wings: They have two pairs of thin, see-through wings that zip together to fly super fast.

Legs: Six legs! Their back legs are special because they have little "pollen baskets" to carry pollen back to the hive.

Abdomen: This is the back part of the bee.

This is where the stinger is. Bees only sting if they feel they or their hive are in danger. It's their way of protecting themselves. After a honeybee stings, it sadly dies, so it's a last resort for them.

Why are Bees SO Important? The Big "P" Word!
Bees are famous for one incredible job: POLLINATION.

What is Pollination? It's how plants make new seeds to grow more plants. Flowers have a powder called pollen. For the flower to turn into a fruit or a vegetable, the pollen needs to be moved from one part of the flower to another.

How do bees help? When a bee lands on a flower to drink sweet nectar (their food), pollen from the flower sticks to their fuzzy bodies. When they fly to the next flower, some of that pollen rubs off. It's like the bee is delivering a special package for the flower!

Thanks to bees, we have many of our favorite foods!
Think about apples, strawberries, blueberries, pumpkins, cucumbers, and almonds. No bees? Almost no fruits, nuts, or vegetables! They are essential for our existence.

The Buzz about Different Types of Bees
There are over 20,000 different kinds of bees! But let's meet the three most famous ones you'll find in a honeybee hive:

The Queen Bee:

Job: She is the mother of the entire hive. Her main job is to lay eggs—thousands of them! There is usually only one queen.

The Worker Bees:

Job: These are all female bees, and they do ALL the work! They are nurses, cleaners, builders, guards, and most importantly, foragers (food collectors). They are the ones you see flying from flower to flower.

Fun Fact: Almost all the bees you see are worker bees.

The Drone Bees:

Job: These are the male bees. Their only job is to mate with a new queen. They don't have stingers and they don't collect food.

Hexagonal Honeycomb: Bees make wax from their bodies and build little six-sided rooms called cells. These hexagons are a perfect shape—they use the least amount of wax to hold the most amount of honey!

Baby Bees (Larvae): The queen lays eggs in some cells.

Honey: Worker bees store sweet honey in other cells to eat during the winter.

Pollen: They also store pollen, which is full of protein, to feed the baby bees.

How Do Bees Make Honey?
This is a cool process!

Collect Nectar: A worker bee drinks nectar from a flower using her long tongue.

Store it: She stores the nectar in a special "honey stomach" separate from her real stomach.

Pass it Along: Back at the hive, she passes the nectar to another worker bee by regurgitating (spitting) it up.

Evaporate Water: The bees fan the nectar with their wings to make the water in it evaporate. This makes the nectar thick and sticky.

Cap it with Wax: Once the honey is perfect, they seal the cell with a tiny wax cap to save it for later!

It takes visits to two million flowers to make just one pound of honey. That's a lot of work for a tiny bee!
Fun Facts to Buzz About!
Bees can fly up to 15 miles per hour.

To make one jar of honey, worker bees fly a total distance equal to going around the world three times!

Bees communicate by dancing! They do a "waggle dance" to tell other bees where to find the best flowers.

The buzzing sound comes from their wings beating 11,000 times per second!

The story teaches readers to **embrace their individuality** and not let others' expectations or stereotypes define them. video_title: 👧🏻 My Body Belongs to Me From My Head to My Toes
description:
My Body Belongs to Me from My Head to My Toes (The Safe Child, Happy Parent Series) created by Pro Familia, illustrated by Dagmar Geisler. Read by Riko.


As a child, there are constantly people trying to pick you up, hug you, or tickle you. Sometimes, though, children fall victims to people who try to touch them inappropriately.

But how do you tell someone, most likely an adult, that you don’t want to be touched? Or, if it has already happened, how do you tell an adult you trust about what happened? You’re only a child, and they’re the adults. Why would they believe you?

My Body Belongs to Me from My Head to My Toes is an educational tool to help instill confidence in children when it comes to their bodies. The narrative of the story is led by a girl named Clara, who encourages kids to say “no” if they are uncomfortable with physical contact. The narrator gives readers tips about what they can say or do to avoid unwanted physical contact, or how to tell the right people in the event it has already occurred.

My Body Belongs to Me from My Head to My Toes is an invaluable resource that gives children a voice in uncomfortable situations.

video_title: Addy Matic and the Toasterrific! By Curtis Mark Williams
description:
Addy-matic and the Toasterrific is a humorous, rhyming picture book about a girl who attempts to automate a simple task by building a complex, Rube Goldberg-esque chain reaction machine.

Having to wake up early, Adeline (call her Addy, but a warning: just don't call her in the morning) is not the least bit in the mood to make her own food, so she decides to find a way to automate getting toast made on a plate. Using things around her, she builds a grand creation of perfect automation she calls the effortless Toasterrific!...but will it work?

Young readers will feel empowered by the hero of the story, a young girl, who is faced with a dilemma: “How to automate the task of toasting bread?” Her passion for problem solving compels her to single-handedly design and build an ironically complicated machine called the Toasterrific.

The relevant content of this book is important because it celebrates an imaginative young girl’s love of engineering while echoing the concepts of STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Math).

Additionally, in a very straight-forward manner, the book exemplifies how simple machines work and how certain objects meant for one purpose might be used in a completely original way.

video_title: MASK - Volcano of Venom - Read Along Story Book - Digital HD - (Mobile Armored Strike Kommand)
description:
MASK - Read Along Story Book and Audio Cassette for MASK - Volcano of Venom - The main premise revolved around the fight between an underground task force called M.A.S.K. (Mobile Armored Strike Kommand) against a criminal organization called V.E.N.O.M. (Vicious Evil Network of Mayhem). After its initial launch in 1985, the franchise spawned a variety of products, including four series of action figures, an animated television series, video games and comics.

► Comics

The first M.A.S.K. comics were three mini-comics produced by Kenner that were packaged with the vehicles from the first series of toys in 1985. After the success of the franchise, DC Comics picked up the rights and produced a special insert which appeared in several comic books dated September 1985. A four-issue miniseries was begun in December 1985. This was soon followed by a regular series of comics that lasted nine issues. Two M.A.S.K. Annual comics were produced as well (1986 and 1987).

A selection of the DC strips were reprinted in the UK, by Grandreams in Christmas Annuals, which also featured original text stories. Fleetway's M.A.S.K. comic magazine, initially published fortnightly before moving to a weekly pattern, featured entirely new plots produced by British writers and artists, in the standard mostly black and white short strip format of British comics. The stories were in their own continuity, not connected to either the cartoon series or DC/Grandreams comics. There was a notable difference in the comics in that Venom knew the identities of M.A.S.K. agents, whereas in the first cartoon series they did not. This weekly title lasted 80 issues before merging with the second incarnation of Eagle.

In 2011, a re-imagined M.A.S.K. version was presented at the New York Comic Con by Hasbro Toys. This version still featured Matt Trakker as the leader of the team. However, M.A.S.K. is presented as a rogue quasi-law enforcement agency battling corruption in Detroit, instead of fighting against V.E.N.O.M. Trakker himself is a police officer instead of a wealthy philanthropist. The rest of the team was different as well. This version was written by former IDW comics senior editor and current Hasbro in-house writer, Andy Schmidt. However this series was never released.

In 2016, M.A.S.K. was re-introduced as part of the Revolution crossover from IDW. Matt Trakker is African-American in this new version. The ongoing series started on November 2016.

► Video games

Screenshot from the Commodore 64 version of M.A.S.K. III: Venom Strikes Back
Beginning in 1987, British software house Gremlin Graphics released a trilogy of computer games based on the M.A.S.K. franchise for various eight-bit computer formats.

The first game, MASK I, was a vertically-viewed 2D game in which the player controls the Thunderhawk vehicle. The premise of the game is that V.E.N.O.M. have propelled Boulder Hill into a time vortex, and the player must rescue the other members of the M.A.S.K. team by collecting and re-assembling parts of a scan key, which then directs the player to the location of the missing personnel. The game received mostly favorable reviews at the time, although it was noted by some that the tie-in to the franchise was quite tenuous and only the graphics, rather than the storyline and gameplay, connected it to the M.A.S.K. franchise.

The second game, MASK II, also released in 1987, was a 2D horizontal scrolling shoot-em-up. The game featured many more of the M.A.S.K. vehicles, and included a selection process in which the player chose which vehicles to use before the game began. Only one vehicle could be controlled at a time but these could be quickly interchanged. Again, the game was received favorably in the press, where it was noted that it was a better tie-in to the franchise than the first, because it featured more of the vehicles.

The final game in the trilogy MASK III – Venom Strikes Back was released in 1988 and was a 2D horizontal shoot-em-up. The premise of the game is that V.E.N.O.M. have kidnapped Scott Trakker and are holding him on the moon. The player controls Matt Trakker (unrecognizable in a space suit with helmet) through a series of static screens featuring platform puzzles and obstacles which must be overcome using the powers of the various masks. The player can hold up to four masks at a time, but can only use the power of one at a time. The masks can also be exchanged at certain points in the game. This game received the best reviews of the trilogy, despite the deviation from the franchise's storyline and style.

All three M.A.S.K. games were released for the ZX Spectrum, Commodore 64 and Amstrad CPC formats, while the second and third games were also released for the MSX format.

video_title: The Greedy Triangle (Shape Shifter-explore geometric concepts in a fun & engaging way) #kids #story
description:
The Greedy Triangle by Marilyn Burns is a children's book that combines math and storytelling to explore geometric concepts in a fun and engaging way. Here's an overview of its theme, summary, and lesson:

### **Theme**
The central theme of *The Greedy Triangle* is **change and self-discovery**. The story uses the concept of shapes and their properties to teach children about geometry while also conveying a deeper message about being content with who you are and embracing your unique qualities.

---

### **Summary**
The story follows a triangle who feels bored with its life and wants to experience something new. The triangle visits a "Shape Shifter" and asks to have its sides and angles changed so it can become a different shape. With each transformation, the triangle becomes a new shape (e.g., a quadrilateral, pentagon, hexagon, etc.) and enjoys the new experiences that come with it. However, as the triangle gains more sides and angles, it begins to feel uncomfortable and realizes that life was simpler and more fulfilling when it was just a triangle. In the end, the triangle decides to return to its original shape, appreciating its simplicity and uniqueness.

### **Lesson**
The book teaches two key lessons:
1. **Mathematical Lesson**: It introduces children to the properties of shapes, such as the number of sides and angles, and how changing these properties transforms one shape into another.
2. **Life Lesson**: It conveys the importance of being content with who you are. The triangle's journey shows that constantly seeking change or wanting to be something else can lead to dissatisfaction, and sometimes, simplicity and self-acceptance are the keys to happiness.

*The Greedy Triangle* is a great tool for teaching geometry concepts to young learners while also imparting a valuable life lesson about self-acceptance and the beauty of being unique.

video_title: Winston's Forever Blanket | Read Aloud by Reading Pioneers Academy
description:
The Bond of Love after loss!
The loss of a friend, family member, or pet can be devastating to a child. Dealing with grief can be difficult as children do not understand how to mourn or begin the healing process.

In this heartwarming story, a little bunny named Winston, holds onto a special blanket given to him by his beloved mother. This magical blanket is his source of comfort and security, during times of fear and uncertainty, a symbol of their unbreakable bond. But one day, disaster strikes, and Winston's cherished blanket goes missing, leaving him in a state of panic and despair.
Spotting the distressed bunny, a team of compassionate and understanding animals join him in his search without hesitation.

Parents, educators, grief counselors and psychologists agree that this children’s book about grief and loss is a powerful tool to help children create their own special memories. Carrying similar messages such as The Invisible String, The Rabbit Listened, God Gave Us Heaven, and The Memory Box, children will have a better understanding of the special bond that can never be broken even after loss.

This extraordinary keepsake gift is also a great conversation starter in class. Children can learn to empathize with those experiencing loss as well as think of creating their own memory box.

With beautiful, colorful illustrations, this book is perfect for children aged 4 to 8 and a great tool for grief counselors, therapists, psychologists, parents and teachers.

Grab your copy of Winston's Forever Blanket today before the price goes up, and discover the healing power of Love after Loss

video_title: 'We Were Lucky': Life Philosophy Learned After The Holocaust | Story of the Week
description:
Abe and Esther Schuster grew up children of Holocaust survivors. Their father, Judel, lost his parents and sister in the Sarny ghetto. Pauline, their mother, lost her entire family — they were murdered during the Nazi occupation of Uman, then part of the Soviet Union.

Pauline and Judel met in Stalingrad and married there in 1945, shortly before they entered a displaced persons camp in Italy. Four years later, they left Europe and arrived by boat in New York to begin a new life.

At StoryCorps, Abe and Esther sat down to remember their parents’ philosophy of life. And as Abe’s high school math teacher would learn, that didn’t always mean following the rules.

video_title: The Construction Alphabet Book (informative) #educational #toddlers #kindergarten #kidstory #books
description:
The Construction Alphabet Book
Author: Jerry Pallotta
Illustrator: Rob Bolster
Publisher: Charlesbridge Publishing
Recommended Age Range: 3-7 years old

Overview and Concept
This book uses the framework of the alphabet to introduce young readers to a wide variety of construction equipment and vehicles. From common sights like a bulldozer to more specialized machines like a knuckleboom loader, each letter of the alphabet is represented by a different piece of equipment.

The genius of the book is that it goes beyond a simple "A is for Ambulance" format. Pallotta provides engaging, factual descriptions that explain what each machine does, how it works, and why it's important on a construction site.

Structure and Content
Alphabet Format: Each page focuses on one letter (e.g., "A is for Aerial Lift," "B is for Bulldozer").

Detailed Descriptions: For every machine, the text describes its function in a simple yet informative way. For example, it doesn't just say "this is a crane," it explains how the crane's boom and hook are used to lift heavy steel beams.

Illustrations: Rob Bolster's illustrations are a key highlight. They are bright, clean, detailed, and visually appealing to children. The machines are often shown in action, digging, lifting, or moving dirt, which helps children understand their purpose.

Comparison and Contrast: A particularly engaging feature is that Pallotta often compares machines. For the letter C, he introduces the Crane but then also shows a smaller "Cherry Picker" (a type of crane), explaining the differences between them. This makes the book more dynamic and educational.

Humor and Fun Facts: The author includes light humor and interesting facts to keep children engaged. For instance, he might joke about a machine's funny name or unusual look.
The Construction Alphabet Book is far more than just an ABC book. It's a brilliantly executed, informative, and highly engaging nonfiction picture book that turns a child's fascination with big trucks into a genuine learning opportunity. It's a frequent favorite and a highly recommended addition to any young child's library.

description:
The Shape of Me and Other Stuff by Dr. Seuss. Read by Riko.

Subtitled "Dr. Seuss's Surprising Word Book," The Shape of Me and Other Stuff certainly lives up to its billing. In this delightful book, first published in 1973, kids are encouraged to ponder shapes they may never have considered before: "Just think about the shape of beans and flowers and mice and big machines!" Hansel and Gretel are lost and starving in the deep dark forest, even stale bread and scary stepmother Other will be better than endless trees. Then they buy a house made of chocolate and cake surely it’s too good to be true….

The tale of Hansel and Gretel teaches a number of important morals. One of the most important lessons is that patience and cleverness can assist you in overcoming challenging obstacles and difficulties. Despite being abandoned in the forest and facing the possibility of being eaten by a witch, Hansel and Gretel were able to escape and find their way back home by using their wits and working together.


Another lesson is the value of family and the link between siblings. Hansel and Gretel demonstrated how much they loved and cared for each other, and how their love and support for one another helped them survive.

Furthermore, the story emphasizes the value of being resourceful and making the most of what you have. Hansel’s brilliant idea of leaving a pebbles trail guided them back home.

It can also be viewed as a reflection of poverty and the moral confusion it creates for families and society.

The narrative also demonstrates that sometimes a tough or painful solution to a situation is required for the greater benefit. The woodcutter’s wife’s decision to forsake her children was tough, but it was necessary for the family’s survival.

The Seed: Little Boo begins as a humble seed, nestled in the earth. It dreams of becoming truly frightening, just like the other pumpkins.
Seasonal Challenges: As the seasons change, Little Boo tries to scare various characters—a snowflake in winter, bees in spring, and even a watering can. But alas, it doesn’t succeed in being scary.
Patience and Persistence: Encouraged by a friendly swirl of wind, Little Boo persists. The wind advises patience, promising that it will be scary soon enough.
The Transformation: Finally, as Halloween approaches, Little Boo blossoms into a grinning jack-o’-lantern. Its “boo” now terrifies all who pass by.
Tim Zeltner’s layered paintings effectively convey the changing seasons, creating a natural world teeming with anthropomorphic snowflakes, garden boots, and grasshoppers. The story shares similarities with Margaret Wise Brown’s “The Fierce Yellow Pumpkin,” but it stands on its own as a shorter yet equally delightful option for young readers.

“Little Boo” is perfect for children who eagerly anticipate growing up and facing their own transformations. With its gentle message and captivating illustrations, this book is sure to enchant both kids and adults alike. (AI generated).

video_title: Wherever You Are My Love Will Find You (extra reassurance)#educational #toddlers #kindergarten #kids
description:
"Wherever You Are: My Love Will Find You" is a beloved children's picture book written by Nancy Tillman. It's a beautiful and heartfelt reassurance of a parent's (or caregiver's) unconditional and ever-present love.

Here is a detailed overview of the book.

Overview of "Wherever You Are: My Love Will Find You"
Author & Illustrator: Nancy Tillman
Genre: Children's Picture Book (Ages 1-4, but all ages)
Theme: Unconditional love, comfort, reassurance, the bond between parent and child.

Synopsis
The book is not a story with a plot in the traditional sense. Instead, it is a lyrical poem spoken from the perspective of a parent to a child. It serves as a promise that no matter where the child goes, what they do, or who they become, the parent's love will always be there to guide, comfort, and protect them.

The narrator imagines the child in various grand, whimsical, and sometimes challenging scenarios—traveling to far-off lands, climbing tall mountains, playing with elephants, or feeling small and scared. In each instance, the message is the same: the parent's love is a constant, invisible force that will find them.

Key Messages and Quotes
The book is filled with memorable, soothing lines that have made it a favorite for bedtime reading:

"I wanted you more than you ever will know, so I sent love to follow wherever you go." This opening line sets the tone for the entire book.

"It's as high as you wish it. It’s as big as you need. My love can be larger than the largest stampede."

"If you’re still my small child or all grown and tall, my love will find you, no matter how tall."

"So climb any mountain… climb up to the sky! My love will find you. My love can fly!"

The book famously ends with the powerful, reassuring line: "You are loved. You are loved. You are loved," they said."

Illustrations
Nancy Tillman's illustrations are a huge part of the book's magic and appeal. They are:

Dreamlike and Magical: They feature soft, ethereal backgrounds and fantastical elements like children riding on the backs of elephants, floating with balloons, or talking to bears.

Whimsical and Imaginative: The art perfectly captures the boundless imagination of childhood and the boundless nature of a parent's love.

Comforting: The use of soft light, gentle colors, and serene expressions on the characters' faces creates a deeply calming and secure atmosphere.

Why It's So Popular
Universal Message: It perfectly articulates the deep, unconditional love a parent feels for their child, a sentiment that resonates with caregivers everywhere.

Comforting for Children: It addresses a core childhood anxiety: separation and the fear of not being loved. The book provides tangible, imaginative reassurance.

Beautiful Gift Book: It is a very common gift for baby showers, christenings, birthdays, and especially from a parent to a child.

Soothing Bedtime Read: The rhythmic, poetic text and peaceful illustrations make it an ideal book to read before sleep.

Ideal For:
Parents and Grandparents to read to their young children.

Gifting for new babies, birthdays, holidays, or just to say "I love you."

Children who may be experiencing anxiety, a new sibling, starting school, or any transition where they need extra reassurance.

Any occasion where you want to express a love that is constant and everlasting.

In essence, "Wherever You Are: My Love Will Find You" is more than a book; it's a cherished promise put into words and pictures. It's a timeless keepsake that families read over and over again.

Click to download the book or leave a review: https://amzn.to/3Ax7y4u

A simple and effective emotions and feelings picture book read along about insecurity, confidence, self-esteem, growth mindset, identity and belonging. Teach toddlers, preschoolers, kindergarteners and even young adults how to transform insecurity, embarrassment and inadequacy into confidence, self-esteem, assertiveness, perspective and growth mindset.

Insecurity is a Seed is the best character education and social emotional learning (SEL) children's book to help kids and adults transform insecurity into confidence and self-esteem. Perfect children's book for preschool, elementary school, middle school or even high school students who struggle with identity and belonging, social isolation, exclusion, bullying, teasing, insecurity, embarrassment, perfectionism, performance anxiety or inadequacy.

The straightforward emotion and feelings book is applicable to all insecurity triggers, while the illustrations also make this a perfect book for kids struggling with identity and belonging, perfectionism, or feeling unique, different or not good enough. Perfect for boys, girls, early readers, primary school students, toddlers or any child or adult age 2 - 12+.

Insecurity is a Seed is part of a social emotional learning children's book series, created by a Special Education teacher, curriculum writer and mother of two young boys, to help children, parents and educators develop their emotional regulation skills.

Social Emotional Learning standards are quickly becoming mandatory in many school districts. Teach your children to manage negative emotions in positive and productive ways with this fun and simple emotional intelligence and self-regulation book. Every book includes a reading response activity for any teacher, parent, social worker, school counselor or therapist to lead a no prep discussion or lesson about identity, belonging, insecurity, confidence, growth mindset and self esteem.

If you like Stand Tall Molly Lou Melon, Giraffes Can't Dance or Todd Parr's It's Okay to be Different or The Okay Book, you will love this short and sweet picture book that comforts and teaches even the youngest readers confidence, self-esteem, growth mindset, optimism, it's okay to be unique, and a sense of perspective that "it gets better". With the emotional regulation concepts of the Ninja Life Hacks, Slumberkins or A Little Spot of Emotion book sets, Insecurity is a Seed is the best confidence and self-esteem book to teach children of all ages - from toddlers and preschoolers to teens and young adults - to overcome insecurity despite bullying, teasing or feeling different or not good enough.

Critical Review: A simple, powerful book for building confidence

"It's no small task to write a book for little children on confidence. Insecurity is a tough concept even for us adults. But this book, through simple words and engaging pictures, gives parents a starting point for raising their kids to be confident and resilient. The book includes questions at the end that parents and grandparents can use to reinforce the lesson of the book."

video_title: THE VOICE THAT WON THE VOTE: HOW ONE WOMAN’S WORDS MADE HISTORY  Informational Kids Book Read Aloud
description:
A vote is a voice. For nearly 75-years, American women campaigned for voting rights – the right to have a voice in their own government. They held meetings, marched in parades, and made speeches – all to no avail. But in 1920, that was about to change. Women’s suffrage came down to the vote in Tennessee. If the Tennessee legislature approved the Nineteenth Amendment, it would be ratified, giving all American women the right to vote.

Tennesseean Febb Burn was smart, and strong-willed--and determined to have a voice. As the vote approached, she wrote a letter -- a letter that would tip the scales toward equality. The historic moment would be decided by a single vote. This is the little-known story of Febb, her son Harry, and the letter that gave American women a voice. Let’s experience the magic of reading as I read aloud “The Voice That Won The Vote: How One Women’s Words Made History,” written by Elisa Boxer and Illustrated by Vivien Mildenberger and learn about this historic moment in our history.

Kids should read at least 20-minutes a day.” Let’s read this wonderful story together, with Mrs. K. Enhanced with our new Magic Reading Table, background music and sound effects to make this great story, come alive!

description:
Caveboy Crush by Beth Ferry), illustrated by Joseph Kuefler. Read by Riko.

Neander is a young caveboy. He spends his days doodling on cave walls, chasing mammoth butterflies, and playing with his pet rock, Rock. But one day, he meets Neanne—and he’s CRUSHED! She’s short, she’s hairy, she’s perfect! Neander does everything he can think of to get Neanne’s attention. He picks a bouquet for her from the Field of the Bees. He fetches a conch shell for her from the Waves of Salt. As Neander’s gestures get grander and grander, Neanne remains unimpressed. But then Neander hatches the grandest gesture of all, and it’s Neanne’s turn to do some crushing. From Beth Ferry and Joseph Kuefler comes this sweet celebration of first love—perfect for Valentine’s Day and read-alouds all year long.

video_title: I Am Smart - A Positive Power Story - Kids Read Aloud Audiobook

When his teacher announces that there will be a science fair in a few weeks, the young boy in I Am Smart is worried. He doesn't like science. Science is hard! Perfect for parents, classroom or homeschool teachers who want a no prep read along activity or educational videos for effortless no prep learning activities via educational screen time.

All the picture books will give children the opportunity to practice every K-2 reading skill while also introducing the following social emotional learning skills: Empathy, sharing, how to be a good friend, listening skills, gratitude, overcoming disappointment, responding to challenges/obstacles, growth mindset, adapting to change, self-esteem, being yourself, individuality, anti-bullying, assertiveness, optimism, positive attitude.

For the drawing activity, drawing materials (paper and pencil, markers, crayons, etc.) are recommended. If materials are not available or children are enjoying the video on-the-go, they can use the drawing tool on their device’s notepad (Notes app), type their response (with adult help) or come back to the activity later. 

My primary goal is for you to complete this video knowing your child has mastered important social emotional learning and early reading skills, and is now prepared to succeed academically and socially in kindergarten, first, grade, third grade, elementary school and beyond. video_title: The Hole Story of The Doughnut (high-seas adventure and creative thinking) Kids Picture Read Aloud
description:
“The Hole Story of the Doughnut”.
In 1843, a young fourteen-year-old named Hanson Gregory embarked on a seafaring adventure as a cabin boy aboard the schooner Achorn from Rockport, Maine. Little did he know that his knack for creative problem-solving would lead to the invention of one of the world’s most beloved pastries: the doughnut.

Hanson Crockett Gregory, a seafaring cook, is credited with inventing these sweet fried treats. His ingenious solution to a common problem resulted in the iconic doughnut shape we know today. But how did it happen?

Picture this: hungry sailors on board the Achorn craved a tasty treat, but the traditional fried cakes they enjoyed were often raw in the center. Hanson had an idea. He decided to punch a hole in the center of the dough before frying it. This simple yet brilliant modification ensured that the dough cooked evenly, leaving no uncooked center. And just like that, the doughnut was born!

The whimsical and inventive cut-paper illustrations in this delightful picture book add a taste of magic to the story. Alongside the narrative, you’ll find an extensive bibliography, an author’s note, and a timeline, making it a perfect read for curious minds.

So next time you savor a doughnut, remember the high-seas adventure and creative thinking that brought this delectable treat into existence! (AI generated).

”I Choose to Calm My Anger” is a story with social-emotional learning (SEL) in mind. It has been praised by teachers and therapists worldwide.
This story told from Jackson’s point of view will help open your child's mind to what it feels like to be angry and how to deal with it. Jackson will teach your child how we are empowered to change our mindset and how we deal with life’s setbacks.
With Jackson in real-life examples, your child will learn to develop their understanding of their own emotions. Throughout the story, Jackson will show you how it feels to be angry and then how to cope.

Where can you plant a garden?

Do you have space do dig in the ground or to place a small or large pot to grow one or more plants?

Herbs like basil, dill, rosemary, oregano and thyme and vegetables like scallions, cherry tomatoes, carrots or peas grow easily in pots inside on a sunny windowsill or anywhere outside.

video_title: From Seed to Pumpkin (celebrates the wonder of nature) #toddlers #kindergarten #kids #educational
description:
“From Seed to Pumpkin” is a delightful children’s picture book that takes young readers on an enchanting journey through the life cycle of pumpkins. Written by Wendy Pfeffer and illustrated by James Graham Hale, this book is part of the Let’s-Read-and-Find-Out Science 1 series. Let’s explore the magic of pumpkins together:

The Story:
In this colorfully illustrated nonfiction picture book, readers discover how pumpkins grow from a tiny yellow seed to a plump, orange pumpkin.
The book introduces the concept of plant life cycles, making it an engaging environmental science read for early elementary-age kids.
What to Expect:
The book is a Level 1 Let’s-Read-and-Find-Out, which means it’s perfect for children in the primary grades.
It answers questions like:
How do plants use roots to drink water from the ground?
What happens as a pumpkin seed sprouts and grows?
How can we roast pumpkin seeds for a tasty snack?
The illustrations are captivating, making the learning experience both informative and enjoyable.
Why We Love “From Seed to Pumpkin”:
It’s hands-on and visual, appealing to curious young minds.

video_title: Chairs on Strike (powerful lesson about kindness and respect) #toddlers #kindergarten #stories #kids
description:
Chairs on Strike is a playful and didactic children's picture book,  and written by Jennifer Jones. It is part of a popular series that includes Pencils on Strike, Crayons on Strike, and others.

The book uses humor and a relatable scenario to teach children about respect, responsibility, and the importance of taking care of their belongings.

Plot Summary
The story begins with a classroom of chairs deciding they have had enough! They are tired of the mistreatment from the students and collectively go on strike. They refuse to be sat on until their demands are met.

Through a series of rhyming verses, the chairs list their grievances. These include:

Being Tipped Back: "No more leaning back in your chair, it's not safe and it's not fair!"

Being Dragged: "Don't drag us roughly on the floor, our legs are sore, we can't take more!"

Being Used as a Step-Stool: "We are not a step or stair, so please don't stand up on our chair!"

General Rough Treatment: They complain about being wobbled, kicked, and written on.

The chairs present their case directly to the readers (the children), explaining how this mistreatment makes them feel sad, broken, and unappreciated. The strike causes a problem everyone can understand: the students have nowhere to sit!

The resolution comes when the children realize the error of their ways. They apologize to the chairs and promise to be more kind and careful. The chairs, seeing the sincere change of heart, agree to end their strike and return to their important job of supporting the students.

Themes and Message
Respect for Property: The core message is about treating classroom (and by extension, home) supplies with care.

Empathy: The book encourages children to see things from the perspective of inanimate objects, fostering a sense of empathy. The chairs are given feelings and voices.

Consequences: It clearly shows that actions have consequences. Mistreating the chairs leads directly to the problem of having nowhere to sit.

Responsibility: It teaches children to take responsibility for their actions and to correct their behavior when they make a mistake.

Problem-Solving: The story presents a conflict and shows how it can be resolved through communication, apology, and changed behavior.

Target Audience
The book is ideally suited for children in Preschool through 2nd or 3rd grade (approximately ages 3-8). It is a perfect read-aloud book for teachers at the beginning of the school year to set classroom expectations or for parents dealing with similar issues at home.

Reception
The On Strike series is generally very well-received by its target audience: teachers, parents, and librarians. It is praised for:

Presenting a important lesson in a fun, memorable, and non-preachy way.

Engaging children with colorful and expressive illustrations.

Using catchy rhymes that make it enjoyable to read aloud.

Effectively addressing a common classroom management issue.

In Conclusion
Chairs on Strike by Jennifer Jones is a clever and effective tool for social-emotional learning. It turns a common behavioral issue into a humorous story with a powerful lesson about kindness and respect, making it a valuable addition to any young child's bookshelf or classroom library.

video_title: Sick Simon by Dan Krall (Personal Health & Hygiene) #toddlers #kindergarten #education #kidsbooks
description:
"Sick Simon" is a clever, humorous, and slightly gross picture book written and illustrated by Dan Krall. It tells the story of a young boy named Simon who is excited to be sick.

Unlike most kids, Simon loves everything about being ill—the days off school, the cozy blankets, and the special treatment. He's so enthusiastic that he actively tries to stay sick by embracing his germs. He coughs without covering his mouth, doesn't wash his hands, and even kisses his family members goodnight, proudly spreading his germs everywhere.

The story takes a fantastical turn when Simon's germs—personified as cute, googly-eyed monsters—start talking to him. They reveal that they are using him as a paradise and a vehicle to spread to his friends, family, and entire town. At first, Simon is proud of his "accomplishment," but he soon realizes the consequences: his whole class, his teacher, and even his family get sick, ruining a much-anticipated field trip.

In the end, Simon decides to fight back against his germs by adopting healthy habits, ultimately learning how to be sick responsibly.

Themes and Lessons
"Sick Simon" is a powerful tool for teaching children about health and empathy in a way that is engaging and memorable, not preachy.

1. Personal Health and Hygiene
This is the most direct theme. The book serves as a fun, illustrated guide to basic hygiene practices. It explicitly shows why actions like covering your coughs, washing your hands, and using tissues are important.

Lesson: Good hygiene isn't just a rule; it's a way to keep yourself and others healthy.

2. Empathy and Community Responsibility
The book brilliantly shifts the focus from the individual ("I get to stay home!") to the community ("Oh no, I got everyone else sick!"). Simon's journey is about understanding that his actions have consequences for those around him.

Lesson: We have a responsibility to our friends, family, and community to try not to spread germs. It's about caring for others.

3. Cause and Effect
Krall masterfully illustrates the chain reaction of sickness. Simon's one set of germs leads to his whole class getting ill, which then cancels a fun event for everyone.

Lesson: Your choices can create a ripple effect, impacting more people than you might realize.

4. Knowledge is Power
The book demystifies germs by giving them a personality. Instead of being an abstract, scary concept, germs are shown as tangible creatures that can be understood and managed. By knowing how germs spread, Simon gains the power to fight them.

Lesson: Understanding how you get sick and how sickness spreads is the first step to preventing it.

How the Book Achieves Its Goal
Humor and the "Gross-Out" Factor: The illustrations of the colorful, slimy germs and Simon's unabashedly snotty behavior are hilarious to children. This "gross" factor grabs their attention and makes the lesson stick far better than a simple lecture.

Personification of Germs: By making the germs cute and giving them voices, the abstract concept of illness becomes concrete and understandable for a young child. It turns a health lesson into a story about a battle between a boy and his microscopic monsters.

Relatable Protagonist: Every child has been sick and can relate to the mixed feelings of misery and the small comforts that come with it. Simon is not a villain; he's just a kid who doesn't understand the bigger picture, making his eventual realization more impactful.

In Summary
"Sick Simon" is more than just a book about washing your hands. It's a story about growing from selfishness to selflessness. It teaches children that being part of a community means looking out for each other, and that sometimes, the simplest acts of hygiene are profound acts of kindness. It's a modern classic for parents and teachers looking for a fun, effective way to discuss health and empathy.

description:
From Shel Silverstein, New York Times bestselling author of Where the Sidewalk Ends and A Light in the Attic, comes a poignant picture book about love and acceptance, cherished for over fifty years. This classic is perfect for both young readers and lifelong fans.

"Once there was a tree...and she loved a little boy."

So begins a story of unforgettable perception, beautifully written and illustrated by the gifted and versatile Shel Silverstein. This moving parable for all ages offers a touching interpretation of the gift of giving and a serene acceptance of another's capacity to love in return.

Every day the boy would come to the tree to eat her apples, swing from her branches, or slide down her trunk...and the tree was happy. But as the boy grew older he began to want more from the tree, and the tree gave and gave and gave. This is a tender story, touched with sadness, aglow with consolation.

The Giving Tree is a meaningful gift for milestone events such as graduations, birthdays, and baby showers.

Shel Silverstein's incomparable career as a bestselling children's book author and illustrator began with Lafcadio, the Lion Who Shot Back. He is also the creator of picture books including A Giraffe and a Half, Who Wants a Cheap Rhinoceros?, The Missing Piece, The Missing Piece Meets the Big O, and the perennial favorite The Giving Tree, and of classic poetry collections such as Where the Sidewalk Ends, A Light in the Attic, Falling Up, Every Thing On It, Don't Bump the Glump!, and Runny Babbit plus Runny Babbit Returns.

video_title: Where Do Babies Come From? - Kids Read Aloud Audiobook
description:
An engaging introduction for very young children to the basic facts of life in a way that is gentle, age-appropriate and accessible.
   Research shows that children are learning about sex at an increasingly young age and often from undesirable sources. The Q&A format, with questions posed in the child’s voice and answers starting simply and becoming gradually more in-depth, allows the adult to guide the conversation to a natural and satisfying conclusion. Additional questions at the back of the book allow for further discussion.
   Child psychologist Dr. Jillian Roberts designed the Just Enough series to empower parents/caregivers to start conversations with young ones about difficult or challenging subject matter. Other books in the series deal with diversity, death, separation and divorce.

video_title: Kids Book Read Aloud: Run Wild by David Covell
description:
Have you ever ran wild? Follow along while we read about an outside adventure in this story! 

If you've found a new favorite I encourage you to get a copy of your own, either through purchase or from the library, to read with your favorite people again and again! If you're looking to enhance the reading material, be sure to check out the Five Bookroot Readings suggested questions below. 

#kidsbooks #kidsbooksreadaloud #ReadAloud

---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Bookroot Readings suggested questions to help dive into this book, learn more about your kiddo and what makes them "Run Wild" and free!

1.  Where do you feel you can "Run Wild" in the great outdoors? After the child answers, you can follow up with, "I feel my imagination comes alive/my mind can take a break and enjoy the moment/my soul feels rejuvenated ______________ (at Lake Superior/Sanibel Island/Grand Tetons/your favorite camping spot/sitting in your garden/saving worms from puddles after a rain/when I walk in the mornings and can feel the sunshine on my face/etc).

2. Which of the five sense do you like using the most when out running wild? I bet getting dirty is a part of the answer! 

3. How many parts of nature can we find in our own neighborhood? Make a list/collect/study:
* trees
* insects
* animals - including footprints, scat that they make, where they sleep, their food chain 
* plants - both wild and purposely planted
* senses - how many senses can we use in our own neighborhood? 

4. What is your favorite weather to "Run Wild" in? After the child answers, you can follow up with when your favorite time to "Run Wild" is and come up with a plan to get out during everyone's favorite! Golden hour and raining are favorite exploration times in our home. 

5. Where should we explore and "Run Wild" next? 

We would like to suggest our "Neighborhood" playlist for books about items/topics that could be found in many neighborhoods to help jump start ideas of studying where we live and learning about topics all around us! https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLtPMxDsug9FhN1LqYqfQb7YvXCDlgkAAy

Mozzie the mosquito lives near a pond, down in the meadow. The most beautiful butterflies flutter there all day long. And everyone adores the butterflies—Mozzie most of all. One day, Mozzie builds up her courage, takes a deep breath, and approaches the butterflies. “Can I flutter around with you?” she asks.
But the butterflies don’t hang out with mosquitos, they say. They only like to be around other butterflies, who look and act like they do. So Mozzie came up with a plan—a plan to become a butterfly herself. But when the unexpected happens, being a butterfly might not be so great. Mozzie might need to simply embrace who she’s been all along.
An inversion of the classic Ugly Duckling narrative, The Mozzie with a Sharp Snozzie is a sweet, non-threatening story about self-confidence, bullying, and feeling comfortable in one’s own skin. Embracing the meaning of her name, Bridges reflects with poignancy and heart on the way one brave little girl stood proud to help build a bridge between all people and pave the path for future generations.

video_title: 6 Kids Fall/Autumn Story Books Collection #kids #toddlers #kindergarten #story #education #reading
description:
All About Autumn (Fall)
Autumn, also known as fall, is one of the four temperate seasons. It marks the transition from the long, warm days of summer to the cold, short days of winter. It is often celebrated for its stunning beauty, harvest abundance, and a unique sense of cozy reflection.

1. The Science Behind Autumn
Why Do Leaves Change Color?
This is the season's most famous magic trick, and it's all about chemistry and sunlight.

Chlorophyll: During spring and summer, leaves are green due to chlorophyll, a pigment that helps trees convert sunlight into food (photosynthesis). It dominates and masks other colors.

Shorter Days & Cooler Temperatures: As daylight shortens and temperatures drop, trees get the signal to prepare for winter. They stop producing chlorophyll.

The Reveal: As the green chlorophyll breaks down and fades, the other pigments that were always present in the leaves are finally revealed:

Yellows & Oranges (Carotenoids): Responsible for the color of corn, carrots, and daffodils. They are present all year but become visible once the green chlorophyll is gone.

Reds & Purples (Anthocyanins): These are produced in the fall from sugars trapped in the leaves. Their intensity depends on the weather—bright, sunny days and cool (but not freezing) nights produce the most brilliant reds.

Why is it Called Both Autumn and Fall?
Fall: Originated in England in the 1500s as a shortening of the phrase "fall of the leaf." It's the most common term in the United States.

Autumn: Comes from the Latin word autumnus. It became the preferred term in England and is used more formally in American English. Both are correct!

When Does it Happen?
Northern Hemisphere: September 22 or 23 (Autumnal Equinox) to December 21 or 22 (Winter Solstice).

Southern Hemisphere: March 20 or 21 (Autumnal Equinox) to June 20 or 21 (Winter Solstice).

The autumnal equinox is the specific moment when the sun crosses the celestial equator, resulting in nearly equal hours of day and night.

2. Cultural Significance and Holidays
Autumn is a season of harvest, gratitude, and remembrance across many cultures.

Harvest Festivals: Celebrating the bounty of the season is a universal theme. Examples include the UK's Harvest Festival, Germany's Erntedankfest, and China's Mid-Autumn Festival (Mooncake Festival).

Halloween (October 31): With Celtic roots in the ancient festival of Samhain, it marks a time when the veil between the living and the spirit world was believed to be thin. 

Día de los Muertos (November 1-2): A vibrant Mexican holiday honoring deceased loved ones with ofrendas (altars), marigolds, sugar skulls, and celebrations.

Thanksgiving ( primarily U.S. and Canada): A major holiday centered around gratitude, family gatherings, and a feast that highlights autumn's harvest (turkey, pumpkins, squash, cranberries, pecans).

3. What to Eat: Autumn's Bounty
The flavors of autumn are rich, warm, and comforting.

Vegetables: Pumpkins, squash (butternut, acorn), sweet potatoes, Brussels sprouts, kale, and beets.

Fruits: Apples, pears, cranberries, pomegranates, and figs.

Nuts: Walnuts, pecans, and hazelnuts are ready for harvesting.

Spices: Cinnamon, nutmeg, cloves, allspice, and ginger—the essential flavors of "pumpkin spice."

4. What to Do: Autumn Activities
The crisp weather invites a unique set of pleasures:

Leaf Peeping: Taking a drive or hike to enjoy the spectacular foliage.

Visit an Orchard or Pumpkin Patch: Go apple picking, navigate a corn maze, and pick out the perfect pumpkin.

Cozy Up: Enjoy the Danish concept of Hygge (hoo-ga)—light candles, curl up with a blanket and a good book, and drink hot apple cider, tea, or a pumpkin spice latte.

Get Baking: Make pies (apple, pumpkin), crisps, and hearty soups and stews.

Enjoy Bonfires: Gather friends and family for a bonfire on a cool evening, perhaps to make s'mores.

5. In the Natural World
Autumn is a time of intense activity and preparation for wildlife.

video_title: Yara my Friend from Syria Read Aloud by Reading Pioneers Academy
description:
This book is about a Syrian girl's first school day in Canada. It depicts her mixed emotions, as she is happy to be in school again but sad to be away from home. The way her new classmates treat her is crucial to her experience. Every parent has an image in their mind of what their children will be like when they grow up. Being a successful adult starts when children are taught the elements of success from a young age. For example, qualities like love, respect, generosity, care, and kindness foster happy and thriving individuals. It may be easy to practice these habits with friends, but much harder to treat new people this way—even for adults. But if children are taught these elements early on, these positive habits can become second nature. Creating an awareness of the world from a young age will help children to become considerate and caring adults to those around them." Yara, My Friend from Syria" emphasizes two main goals: The first is to plant good qualities into children’s pure hearts, so they may become like fruitful trees as they grow up. The second is to increase children’s awareness of global affairs, which may seem upsetting at times but are the reality of the world around us.

video_title: The First Little Red Riding Hood from 1000 Years Ago!
description:
This my own translation of "De puella a lupellis servata," a poem written by the scholar Egbert of Liège 1000 years ago. It tells of a girl given a red tunic by her godfather on her baptismal day, and what happens when some wolves go after her while she is wearing it.

In my translation of this text, I have tried to preserve as much of the literal meaning of the poem as possible while trying to respect its structure of 14 syllables per line. As it did not rhyme in a conventional sense, I chose to include some alliteration to give it a more poetic feel. Here is the original Latin text of the poem:

Quod refero, mecum pagenses dicere norunt,
Et non tam mirum quam ualde est credere uerum:
Quidam suscepit sacro de fonte puellam,
Cui dedit et tunicam rubicundo uellere textam.
Quinquagesima sancta fuit babtismatis huius,
Sole sub exorto quinquennis facta puella;
Progreditur uagabunda sui inmemor atque pericli,
Quam lupus inuadens siluestria lustra petiuit
Et catulis predam tulit atque reliquit edendam.
Qui simul aggressi, cum iam lacerare nequirent,
Ceperunt mulcere caput feritate remota
"Hanc tunicam, mures, nolite," infantula dixit,
"Scindere, quam dedit excipiens de fonte patrinus!"
Mitigat inmites animos deus, auctor eorum.

video_title: NOBODY HUGS A CACTUS by Carter Goodrich read aloud | Kids Picture Book about Friendship
description:
Hank is the prickliest cactus around. He sits in a pot on a window sill that faces the empty desert, which is just how he likes it. So, when all manner of creatures—from tumbleweed to lizard to owl—come to disturb his peace, Hank is annoyed.

video_title: 101 Dalmatians - Read Along Story book - Digital HD - Glenn Close - Jeff Daniels - Joely Richardson
description:
101 Dalmatians Read Along Digital HD Story book - American video game designer Roger Dearly (Jeff Daniels) lives with his pet dalmatian Pongo in London. One day, Pongo sets his eyes on a beautiful female dalmatian named Perdy. After a frantic chase through the streets of London that ends in St. James's Park, Roger discovers that Pongo likes Perdy. Her owner, Anita Campbell-Green (Joely Richardson) falls in love with Roger when they meet. They both fall into the lake as a result of their dogs chasing each other, but they return to Roger's home and Anita accepts his proposal. They get married along with Perdita and Pongo. Anita works as a fashion designer at the House of de Vil. Her boss, the pampered and very glamorous Cruella de Vil (Glenn Close), has a deep passion for fur, going so far as to have a taxidermist, Mr Skinner, skin a white tiger at the London Zoo to make it into a rug for her. Anita, inspired by her dalmatian, designs a coat made with spotted fur. Cruella is intrigued by the idea of making garments out of actual dalmatians, and finds it amusing that it would seem as if she was wearing Anita's dog.

Anita soon discovers that Perdy is pregnant and is then informed by Nanny (Joan Plowright) that she (Anita) is, too, much to her shock. Some time later, Cruella visits their home and expresses contempt upon meeting Roger. Her initial disgust at them having a baby turns to excitement when she finds out Perdy is expecting too. Several weeks later, she returns when a litter of 15 puppies are born and offers Roger and Anita £7,500 for them, but they refuse. She dismisses Anita and vows revenge against her and Roger. She has her henchmen, Jasper and Horace (Hugh Laurie and Mark Williams) break into their home and steal the puppies while Roger and Anita are walking in the park with Pongo and Perdy. Along with 84 others dalmatians that were previously stolen, they deliver them to her ancient country estate, De Vil Mansion. She also hires Skinner to kill and skin them to create her coat.

With the family devastated at the loss of their puppies, Pongo uses the twilight bark to carry the message via the dogs and other animals of England, while Roger and Anita notify the Metropolitan Police. A dog who had witnessed the stolen puppies follows Jasper and Horace to the mansion, and finds all of them inside, before helping them escape under the duo's noses. They make their way to a nearby farm, where they are later joined by Pongo and Perdy. Cruella arrives at the mansion and soon discovers what has happened. Furious, she decides to carry out the job herself, while Jasper and Horace attempt to search for them also. After several mishaps, Jasper and Horace discover nearby police on the hunt for Cruella and her henchmen and hand themselves in, joining Skinner who was beaten earlier while trying to kill Lucky (one of the 15 puppies), who had been left behind. Meanwhile, Cruella tracks the puppies to the farm where they are hiding and tries to retrieve them. However, they outwit her and cause her to fall into a vat of molasses and get thrown through a window into a pig pen. Shortly afterwards, the fleeing dalmatians (including Lucky) are found and sent home via the Suffolk Constabulary, while those looking for Cruella arrive at the farm to arrest her. In the police van, she belittles Jasper, Horace, and Skinner for their incompetence before they are sprayed by a skunk which she had mistaken for her bag. Pongo, Perdy and their puppies are reunited with Roger and Anita.

After being informed that the remaining 84 puppies have no home to go to, as they have not been claimed by their original owners, they decide to adopt them, bringing the total to 101. Roger designs a successful video game featuring dalmatian puppies as the protagonists and Cruella as the villain and they move to the English countryside with their millions. Anita eventually gives birth to her and Roger's first child, and at the very end of the movie, it's implied that she's pregnant with her and Roger's second child.

Bedtime stories and nap time stories for toddlers and older children are a great way to spend time together with family while reading your favorite story.

The Happiest Kid

Written by Sarah Bagley Steele
Illustrated by Elsa Pui Si Lo and Clarice Yunyi Cai

What’s the happiest kid supposed to do when she wakes up not feeling happy? A reassuring picture book debut about recognizing sadness and talking about big feelings.

Sally is usually the happiest kid. She wakes up every morning with a bright sun shining over her bed, and she knows it’s going to be a good day. But one day she wakes up feeling different and there’s a gloomy cloud hanging over her instead. She doesn’t know why it’s there, but she doesn’t want anyone to see it—not her parents, not her teacher, and not her friends—so she hides it away. But as the day goes on, the cloud grows too big and heavy for her to carry, and Sally must find the courage to let it out. 

In this sweet story, Sarah Bagley Steele, Elsa Pu Si Lo, and Clarice Cai offer a gentle reminder that everyone feels sad sometimes, and that’s okay.

video_title: 🗓️ A New Day
description:
A New Day by Brad Meltzer, illustrated by Dan Santat.

Sunday quit, just like that. She said she was tired of being a day. And so the other days of the week had no choice but to advertise: "WANTED: A NEW DAY. Must be relaxing, tranquil, and replenishing. Serious inquires only." Soon lots of hopefuls arrived with their suggestions, such as Funday, Bunday, Acrobaturday, SuperheroDay, and even MonstersWhoResembleJellyfishDay! Things quickly got out of hand . . . until one more candidate showed up: a little girl with a thank-you gift for Sunday. The girl suggested simply a nice day--a day to be kind. And her gratitude made a calendar's worth of difference to Sunday, who decided she didn't need to quit after all.

When we appreciate each other a little bit more, all the days of the week can be brand-new days where everything is possible.

video_title: Llama Llama, Red Pajama (parent's unwavering love) #educational #toddlers #kindergarten #kidsbooks
description:
Llama Llama Red Pajama is a beloved and iconic children's book. Here's a comprehensive overview.

About the Book: Llama Llama Red Pajama
Author and Illustrator: Anna Dewdney
First Published: 2005
Series: It is the first book in the massively popular Llama Llama series.

The Story in a Nutshell
The book tells the story of a young llama, Baby Llama, who is put to bed by his mother. The plot unfolds through simple, rhyming text and highly expressive illustrations:

Bedtime Routine: Mama Llama reads a story, gives Baby Llama kisses, and tucks him into his bed wearing his iconic red pajamas.

Alone and Anxious: Once Mama Llama goes downstairs, Baby Llama feels alone and anxious. He starts to "fret" and "fuss."

The Drama Escalates: He calls out for a drink, then lies in bed worrying when she doesn't come immediately. His imagination runs wild, and his mild fussing turns into a full-blown "llama drama." He pouts, moans, sulks, and eventually throws a tantrum, screaming for his mama.

The Reassurance: Mama Llama comes rushing back, reassuring him that she is always near, even if she's not in the room. She reminds him, "Mama Llama's always near, even if she's not right here."

The Resolution: She gives him one more kiss and tells him softly, "Little Llama, don't you know, Mama Llama loves you so?" Comforted, Baby Llama peacefully falls asleep.

Why It Became a Classic: Themes and Appeal
Relatability for Children: It perfectly captures the common childhood fear of separation and anxiety at bedtime. Every child has felt that moment of panic when a parent leaves the room.

Relatability for Parents: For parents, it's a mirror of the bedtime struggle—the endless calls for water, the stalling, and the sudden tantrums. Mama Llama's patient but firm response is a model for handling these situations with love.

Rhyming Rhythm: The book is written in a perfect, bouncy rhyme scheme that is fun to read aloud and engaging for young listeners.

Emotional Intelligence: Anna Dewdney was a strong advocate for reading as a way to build empathy. The book helps children name their feelings (worry, fear, anger) and shows them that their fears are normal and that they are always loved.

Iconic Illustrations: The characters are incredibly expressive. Baby Llama's face cycles through contentment, worry, sadness, and full-blown panic, allowing children to clearly see and understand his emotions.

The "Llama Llama" Series Legacy
The success of Llama Llama Red Pajama launched a whole series of books tackling common childhood experiences, including:

Llama Llama Mad at Mama (dealing with tantrums while shopping)

Llama Llama Misses Mama (first day of school anxiety)

Llama Llama Holiday Drama (managing excitement and impatience)

Llama Llama and the Bully Goat (handling bullying)

The series also expanded into a Netflix animated show, "Llama Llama" voiced by Jennifer Garner, bringing the characters to an even wider audience.

Fun Facts
Anna Dewdney insisted that her books not have any licensed merchandise for many years, wanting the focus to remain on the books and the act of reading together.

The book's famous line, "Please stop all this Llama Drama!" has become a popular catchphrase among parents.

In her obituary, Dewdney requested that in lieu of memorials, people should "read to a child."

In short, Llama Llama Red Pajama is more than just a book; it's a comforting ritual for millions of families, validating children's emotions and reassuring them of a parent's unwavering love.

With Nazis bombing London every night, it’s time for thirteen-year-old Ken to escape. He suspects his stepmother is glad to see him go, but his dad says he’s one of the lucky ones—one of ninety boys and girls to ship out aboard the SS City of Benares to safety in Canada.

Life aboard the luxury ship is grand—nine-course meals, new friends, and a life far from the bombs, rations, and his stepmum’s glare. And after five days at sea, the ship’s officers announce that they’re out of danger.

Late that night, an explosion hurls Ken from his bunk. They’ve been hit. Torpedoed! The Benares is sinking fast. Terrified, Ken scrambles aboard Lifeboat 12 with five other boys. Will they get away? Will they survive?

Award-winning author Susan Hood brings this little-known World War II story to life in a riveting novel of courage, hope, and compassion. Based on true events and real people, Lifeboat 12 is about believing in one another, knowing that only by banding together will we have any chance to survive.

Roll the Snow: Start by rolling a small snowball on the ground. As you roll, it will pick up more snow and get bigger. This will be the bottom part of your snowman.

Stack Them Up: Place the largest ball at the bottom, the medium one in the middle, and the smallest on top.

Eyes: Small rocks, buttons, or coal.

Clothing: Add a scarf, hat, or even mittens to make your snowman unique.

Snowmen have been around for centuries! People have been building them for fun for a long time.

video_title: Remembering a Mother Gone Missing | Story of the Week
description:
Subscribe to StoryCorps on YouTube: https://storycor.ps/subscribe 

More stories from StoryCorps: https://storycorps.org/
----------
Carolyn DeFord, a Puyallup tribal member, grew up with her mom, Leona Kinsey, in a trailer park in La Grande, Oregon. Twenty years ago, Leona disappeared on her way to her friend’s house, and was never seen again.

She is part of an epidemic of Native American women who have gone missing and never been found.

No one knows exactly how many Native women are missing or murdered, though a report put out by the Urban Indian Health Institute in 2017 cited 5,712 reports of slain or missing Native American women and girls by the National Crime Information Center. Only 116 of those cases were logged into the Department of Justice database for missing persons.

Carolyn came to StoryCorps to remember when she received the phone call that her mother had gone missing.

Originally aired March 29, 2019, on NPR’s Morning Edition.
