description:
Get ready for a heartwarming and hilariously sleepless night on Farmer Brown's farm with "Click, Clack, Peep!" by Doreen Cronin! 🦆🐄 This delightful children's book, perfect for storytime, features a tiny new addition that's keeping everyone awake. This story is read by Dee Hare, Director of the Northeast Regional Library. Join us for a fun readaloud of this beloved kids-book!

In "Click, Clack, Peep!", the always-sleepy Farmer Brown finds his farm in a new kind of uproar. A tiny duckling's constant "peep, peep, peep!" is preventing anyone – from the cows to the hens – from getting any rest. Will Farmer Brown ever catch some sleep? 😴 This charming story, beautifully illustrated by Betsy Lewin, explores themes of new beginnings, the challenges of sleepless nights, and the unexpected joys a new arrival brings. It’s a wonderful readalong experience for young readers and a fantastic addition to any home library. Experience the gentle humor and relatable chaos that only Doreen Cronin can deliver in this captivating kids-book story.

📖 Follow along with our reading:
[00:00] The storyteller, Dee, introduces herself as the director of the Northeast Regional Library
[00:12] She introduces the book she will be reading, "Click, Clack, Peep" by Doreen Cronin and Betsy Lewin
[00:30] Farmer Brown notices the farm is quiet and sees everyone is watching a cracking egg
[01:24] A baby duck hatches from the egg, and it keeps saying "peep, peep, peep"
[01:45] The animals get tired and yawn, trying to get the baby duck to sleep 
[01:58] The animals try different things to help the baby duck sleep, such as singing a lullaby, lowering the shades, and knitting a blanket, but nothing works

video_title: A Camping Spree With Mr. Magee (unexpected adventures) #kids #story #toddlers #kindergarten #reading
description:
"A Camping Spree with Mr. Magee" is a delightful children's picture book written and illustrated by Chris Van Dusen. It was published in 2003 and is the first in a series of humorous adventures featuring the cheerful and somewhat unlucky Mr. Magee and his trusty little dog, Dee.

Plot Summary:
Mr. Magee and his dog Dee set off on a peaceful camping trip, complete with their camper trailer. They find a scenic spot by a mountain lake, roast marshmallows, and enjoy the great outdoors—until a curious bear smells their marshmallows! In an attempt to scare the bear away, Mr. Magee accidentally unhitches his camper, sending it (and Dee inside!) rolling down a hill and straight into the lake!

What follows is a hilarious chain of events involving a waterfall, a fishing boat, and a wild ride that turns their quiet camping trip into an unforgettable adventure. Luckily, everything works out in the end, and Mr. Magee and Dee return home—ready for another escapade (which happens in the sequel, Down to the Sea with Mr. Magee).

Why Kids Love It:
Rhyming text – The story is told in catchy, rhythmic verse that makes it fun to read aloud.

Vivid illustrations – Chris Van Dusen’s bright, retro-style artwork is full of humor and charm.

Exciting yet cozy – The mix of adventure and warmth makes it a great bedtime or storytime book.

Themes:
Unexpected adventures – Even the best-laid plans can go awry!

Problem-solving – Mr. Magee stays calm(ish) and figures things out.

Friendship – The bond between Mr. Magee and Dee is heartwarming.

If you enjoy this book, check out the rest of the Mr. Magee series, as well as Van Dusen’s other works like If I Built a Car and The Circus Ship.

video_title: Oliver & Company - Read Along Story book - Digital HD - Joey Lawrence - Billy Joel - Cheech Marin
description:
Oliver and Company - Read Along Story book - A young cat named Oliver is left alone in a kitten box, while all the other young cats have new owners. A big dog named Dodger shows him how to get food and later Oliver lives with him, his owner Fagin and Fagin's other dogs Tito, Rita, Einstein, and Francis. Fagin has one problem besides being broke he owes a nasty man named Sykes a lot of money. If he can't pay it back he's in big trouble. While Oliver runs into a little girl named Jenny who becomes his new owner which he is happy with and later Sykes sees Jenny as the key for him to get his money. 

Cast and characters from the full movie version were...

Joey Lawrence as Oliver: An orange orphaned kitten who is looking for a home. He joins Fagin's gang of dogs before being taken in by Jenny. He also saves her life from the cruel loan-shark, Sykes.

Billy Joel as Dodger: A charming, mischievous Jack Russell Terrier. He claims to have considerable "street savoir-faire". He is the leader of Fagin's gang of dogs, and is Oliver's first acquaintance, as well as his eventual best friend and guardian. He is the object of Rita's affection.

Cheech Marin as Tito: A tiny yet brave Chihuahua in Fagin's gang. He has a fiery temper for his size, and rapidly develops a crush on Georgette (although she is initially repulsed by him).

Richard Mulligan as Einstein: A gray Great Dane and a member of Fagin's gang. He is named ironically as he is not particularly bright, representing the stereotype that Great Danes are friendly but dull-witted.

Roscoe Lee Browne as Francis: A bulldog with a British accent in Fagin's gang. He appreciates art and theatre, particularly Shakespeare. He also detests anyone abbreviating his name as "Frank" or "Frankie" (which Tito frenquently does).

Sheryl Lee Ralph (Ruth Pointer, singing) as Rita: An Afghan Hound[2] and the only female dog in Fagin's gang. She is street-wise and takes Oliver under her wing.

Dom DeLuise as Fagin: A lowly thief who lives on a barge with his dogs. He desperately needs money to repay his debt with Sykes. Because of his economic situation, he is forced to perform criminal acts such as pick-pocketing and petty theft, but in truth he is kind-hearted and genial.

Taurean Blacque and Carl Weintraub as Roscoe and DeSoto respectively: Sykes's violent Doberman Pinschers who have a volatile history with Dodger and his friends. Roscoe is the apparent leader, while his brother DeSoto seems to be the more threatening of the two. Both of them are killed in the climax by falling onto the electric rail tracks while fighting with Dodger. Roscoe wears a red collar and DeSoto wears one that is blue.

Robert Loggia as Sykes: A mean-spirited, savage loan-shark and shipyard agent who lent a considerable sum of money to Fagin and expects it paid back. He is finally defeated at the end of the film when his car (with him in it) is hit by a train.

Natalie Gregory (Myhanh Tran, singing) as Jennifer "Jenny" Foxworth: A considerate, rich girl who takes care of Oliver.

William Glover as Winston: The Foxworth family's bumbling but loyal butler.

Bette Midler as Georgette: The Foxworth family's show-winning poodle; vain and spoiled, she becomes jealous of Oliver but eventually accepts him and Fagin's gang. At the end, however, she displays considerable attraction to Tito, so much, in fact that she sends him running for his life when she tries to bathe, dress and groom him.

This series is intended to help adults help teach children how to read with phonics. The first two books introduce beginning readers to the vowel sounds chapter by chapter. video_title: The Beeman (Joy, Passion & Importance of Purposeful Work) #toddlers #kindergarten #kidsbooks #school
description:
The Bee Man, tells a warm and gentle story with several interconnected themes.

The primary themes of the book are:

1. The Joy and Importance of Purposeful Work
This is the central theme of the story. The Bee Man loves his work. He finds deep satisfaction in caring for his bees and sharing their honey with his community. The story shows that work isn't just a job; it can be a source of identity, happiness, and connection. When he is forced to stop due to his age, he loses this vital part of himself, which leads directly to the next theme.

2. Intergenerational Friendship and Learning
The story beautifully depicts the relationship between an elderly man and a young, curious boy. The boy isn't just a helper; he is a student. The Bee Man passes on his knowledge, skills, and, most importantly, his passion to the next generation. This theme highlights how wisdom and traditions are preserved not by keeping them to oneself, but by sharing them with eager young minds.

3. The Passing of the Torch / Legacy
Closely tied to intergenerational friendship, this theme is about ensuring that something you love continues after you can no longer do it yourself. The Bee Man's legacy isn't just his bees or his honey; it's his love for beekeeping. By teaching the boy, he ensures that his life's work has a future. The final image of the boy, now grown, tending the bees with his own family shows that the Bee Man's legacy is alive and thriving.

4. Community and Interdependence
The Bee Man doesn't keep his honey for himself; he gives it away to his neighbors. He is a valued and cherished part of his community. When he can no longer perform his role, the community feels the loss (no more honey), and they also show their care for him by sending the boy to check on him. The story illustrates how communities function best when people share their unique gifts and look out for one another.

5. Finding New Ways to Contribute
Even after the boy takes over the physical labor, the Bee Man doesn't become irrelevant. He finds a new, equally important role: that of a teacher and advisor. This is a powerful message about aging, showing that while our capabilities may change, our value and ability to contribute do not diminish—they simply transform.

6. Respect for Nature
Underlying the entire story is a deep respect for the natural world, specifically bees. The book demystifies bees, presenting them not as pests to be feared but as fascinating creatures to be understood and cared for. It introduces young readers to the basics of beekeeping and the vital role bees play in our ecosystem.

In summary, the theme of The Bee Man is about finding purpose through passion, sharing that passion with the next generation, and ensuring that what we love continues to enrich our community even after we step aside. It’s a heartfelt story about legacy, friendship, and the sweet rewards of a life lived in harmony with nature and others.

video_title: The Gift That I Can Give (core message of kindness) #educational #toddlers #kindergarten #kidsbooks
description:
"The Gift That I Can Give" by Kathie Lee Gifford is a wonderful children's book that focuses on the joy of discovering one's unique purpose and the gifts that aren't wrapped in a box.

Here is a detailed overview of the book, perfect for parents, teachers, or anyone considering it as a gift.

Overview of "The Gift That I Can Give"
Author: Kathie Lee Gifford
Illustrator: Julia Seal
Target Age Range: 4-8 years old
Core Theme: Helping children understand that they have unique gifts—like kindness, encouragement, and love—to offer the world right now.

The Story's Message
The book follows a young girl as she explores all the different "gifts" she might possess. She wonders if her gift is something dramatic like being a star athlete, a famous singer, or a brilliant doctor.

The beautiful conclusion she reaches is that the most important gifts aren't about fame or grand achievements. Instead, they are the simple, heartfelt actions she can do every day:

Being a good friend

Sharing

Saying a kind word

Encouraging someone who is sad

Showing love to her family

Helping without being asked

Using her voice to stick up for others

The central message is that every child has something valuable to give the world today, just by being themselves.

Key Themes for Kids
Self-Worth: It assures children that they are special and have inherent value.

Kindness and Empathy: It frames kindness as a superpower and encourages kids to think about how their actions affect others.

Purpose: It introduces the concept of having a purpose in an accessible, non-intimidating way for young children.

Faith-Based Undertone (Subtle): While not preachy, the book has a gentle spiritual message about God giving everyone unique gifts. It's presented in a way that is inclusive and focuses on universal values of love and kindness.

Why It's a Great Gift
Relatable: Kids easily see themselves in the main character's questions and discoveries.

Uplifting and Positive: The colorful illustrations and joyful text create a happy and empowering reading experience.

Spark Conversations: It’s a fantastic conversation starter for parents and children to talk about feelings, kindness, and what makes each child special.

Builds Character: It goes beyond a simple story and serves as a tool for teaching important social-emotional skills.

Perfect for Occasions: It makes a great gift for birthdays, holidays, graduation, or just because.

What Parents and Kids Say
Pros:

The message is powerful and clearly delivered.

The illustrations are bright, engaging, and full of diverse characters.

It's a favorite bedtime story that ends on a warm, positive note.

Many appreciate the faith-based element that focuses on God's love.

Considerations:

A very small number of reviewers who wanted a purely secular book were surprised by the mention of God, though most agree it is handled gently.

Final Verdict
"The Gift That I Can Give" is a heartwarming and empowering book that helps young children build a foundation of kindness, self-confidence, and purpose. It’s a beautiful reminder that the best gifts come from the heart.

It is especially cherished by families looking for children's books with positive, faith-based values, but its core message of kindness is universal and appealing to a wide audience.

Mr. Paul reads aloud "Brave Every Day" by Trudy Ludwig, illustrated by Patrice Barton. This short storybook is an excellent way to introduce the concept of social anxiety, and to help children understand that fear is a normal part of living, which can be managed. This inspiring picture book is equally enjoyable as part of family bedtime at home, or during story time at school.

🎵🎵🎵

About PIPER CHEN SINGS

An empowering story about a girl who turns her performance jitters into confidence when faced with singing a solo at her school concert. Inspired by the childhood experience of award-winning actress Phillipa Soo who originated the role of Eliza in Hamilton.

Piper Chen loves nothing more than to sing. She sings to the sun, and she sings to the moon. She sings to her stuffed animals and with the birds outside her window. So, when her music teacher asks if Piper would like to sing a solo in her school’s Spring Sing, all she can say is “yes!” But as practice continues, doubt and worry creep in and Piper’s confidence wavers. She feels like butterflies are having a dance party in her belly. At home, Piper finds Nai Nai, her grandmother, at the piano. They’ve always shared a love of music, and Piper knows if anyone can help her through the unsettling feeling in her stomach and to shine her brightest at the Spring Concert, it’s Nai Nai.

First time picture book writers and sisters-in-law, Phillipa Soo and Maris Pasquale Doran along with acclaimed illustrator Qin Leng have created a cheerful intergenerational and stunning story that inspires confidence in the face of nervousness

He’s also got a crush on a girl named Jules who he knows he doesn’t have a chance with, because of his size—but he can’t help wondering what if?

Will’s best shot at attracting Jules’s attention is by slaying the Will Monster inside him by changing his eating habits and getting more exercise. But the results are either frustratingly slow or infuriatingly unsuccessful, and Will’s shame begins to morph into self-loathing.

“Did you know that flamingos don’t have teeth?” Questions, facts, and dreams—Ruby René could talk for hours. Once she got going, it was hard for her to stop. It didn’t matter if it was history, science, or the lunch menu—Ruby René had so much to say! But when her teacher called home because she found her sharing distracting, Ruby vowed to keep quiet. video_title: Old Santeclaus with Much Delight - The FIRST Poem Printed about Santa!
description:
This poem was published in 1821 in Volume III of The Children's Friend. This book series was published by William B. Gilley, a printer at No. 92 Broadway in New York. This is the first poem ever printed about the modern-day figure of Santa Claus.

It was published two years before Clement Clark Moore's "A Visit from St. Nicholas," which is much better known, probably because it is more fun. Also, some of the rhymes sound odd today because the modern American accent is very different from that of New York more than 200 years ago! 

This poem is meant to provide moral instruction according to the values of the day. And naughty kids don't get a lump of coal in their stockings -- they get a birch switch!!

“Jack and the Beanstalk” is a classic fairy tale that has captured the imaginations of generations. Let me share the enchanting story with you:

Once upon a time, in a humble cottage, lived a poor widow and her son, Jack. Their only possession was a cow. One day, Jack’s mother instructed him to sell the cow at the market. On his way, Jack encountered a mysterious man who offered him five magic beans in exchange for the cow. Jack, intrigued by the magical promise, accepted the beans.

When he returned home, his mother was furious. She threw the beans out of the window, leaving Jack without dinner. But the next morning, Jack woke up to a remarkable sight: a gigantic beanstalk had sprouted from those very beans! Without hesitation, Jack climbed the beanstalk, ascending into the sky.

At the top, he discovered a kingdom in the clouds, where a giant and his wife resided. The giant’s wife kindly fed Jack, but when the giant returned, Jack hid in fear. The giant’s ominous chant echoed: “Fee-fi-fo-fum, I smell the blood of an Englishman. Be he alive or be he dead, I’ll grind his bones to make my bread!”

Undeterred, Jack visited the giant’s house multiple times. On one occasion, he acquired a hen that laid golden eggs. Another time, he snatched a harp that played beautiful melodies. Each treasure brought wealth to Jack and his mother.

But greed led Jack back to the giant’s castle once more. This time, he encountered the giant’s wrath. The chase ensued, and Jack descended the beanstalk with the hen and the harp. Alas, the beanstalk was cut down, and the giant met his fate.

And so, Jack learned valuable lessons about courage, resourcefulness, and the consequences of his actions. The tale of “Jack and the Beanstalk” continues to inspire wonder and imagination, reminding us that even the smallest among us can achieve great feats.

video_title: Curious George (curiosity leads to unexpected escapades) Kids & Family Picture Story Book Read Aloud
description:
“Curious George” is a beloved children’s book written and illustrated by Margret Rey and H. A. Rey. Published by Houghton Mifflin in 1941, it introduces readers to the delightful adventures of an orphaned monkey named George and his encounters with the enigmatic Man with the Yellow Hat.

Here are some fascinating details about this timeless classic:

Plot: The story begins in the African jungle, where George, a curious little brown monkey, catches the eye of the Man with the Yellow Hat. The Man cleverly captures George by using his oversized yellow hat. He then takes George on a journey—from the jungle to a ship and finally to a big city zoo. Along the way, George’s curiosity leads to unexpected escapades, including a mischievous telephone call to the fire station.
Legacy: For 80 years (as of May 1, 2021), “Curious George” has enchanted readers worldwide. It has sold over 25 million copies and been translated into various languages, including Japanese, French, Afrikaans, Portuguese, Swedish, German, Chinese, Danish, and Norwegian. The book even holds a place in the Indie Choice Book Awards Picture Book Hall of Fame.
Origins: The character of George originated from the 1939 publication of “Cecily G. and the Nine Monkeys”, co-written by the Reys and printed in Paris. London-based publisher Grace Hogarth recognized the magic of George’s story and offered the Reys a four-book deal. She suggested changing the monkey’s name from Fifi to Curious George, and thus, a beloved literary icon was born.
Margret Rey’s Influence: Interestingly, Margret Rey’s name did not appear on early copies of “Curious George” due to gender biases prevalent in children’s literature at the time. Nevertheless, her creative genius shines through in every page.
So, let’s swing from tree branches, explore telephones, and embrace curiosity alongside George and the Man with the Yellow Hat! 🐒(AI generated).

video_title: On The Night You Were Born (Joy and Celebration) #educational #toddlers #kindergarten #kidsbooks
description:
"On the Night You Were Born" is a beloved and heartwarming children's book that has become a modern classic. Here's a detailed overview.

Overview of "On The Night You Were Born"
Author: Nancy Tillman
Publication Date: 2006
Target Age Range: 0-4 years old

The Story's Essence
The book is a beautiful, lyrical celebration of a child's unique and miraculous entry into the world. It’s written in the form of a poetic lullaby, directly addressing the child, and tells them how the entire world—the moon, the stars, the animals, the wind—rejoiced on the night they were born.

The core message is one of unconditional love and the idea that the child is one-of-a-kind, special, and deeply cherished. It’s designed to build a child's self-esteem and sense of belonging from the very beginning.

Key Themes
Uniqueness and Individuality: The book repeatedly emphasizes that there has never been and never will be anyone exactly like the child.

Unconditional Love: It’s a powerful expression of a parent's (or caregiver's) love and wonder at their child.

Joy and Celebration: It paints a magical picture of the natural world pausing to celebrate the birth of this specific child.

Wonder and Magic: The story uses whimsical, fantastical imagery (like polar bears dancing, geese flying home) to create a sense of magic around the child's birth.

Memorable Lines and Imagery
The book is filled with iconic, soothing phrases:

"On the night you were born, the moon smiled with such wonder that the stars peeked in to see you and the night wind whispered, 'Life will never be the same.'"

"For never before in story or rhyme (not even once upon a time) has the world ever known a you, my friend, and it never will, not ever again."

"Heaven blew every trumpet and played every horn on the wonderful, marvelous night you were born."

The imagery of polar bears dancing, geese flying home, and the moon smiling are central to the book's magical feel.

Illustrations
Nancy Tillman's illustrations are a huge part of the book's appeal. They are:

Soft and Dreamlike: Rendered in a soft-focus, almost ethereal style.

Whimsical: Featuring animals, celestial bodies, and nature elements in a gentle, magical way.

Inclusive: Later editions often include illustrations that feature children of different ethnicities, allowing more families to see themselves in the story.

Why It's So Popular
The Perfect Gift: It is arguably the #1 most popular gift book for new babies, baby showers, christenings, and birthdays. It’s often inscribed with a personal message from the giver.

Bedtime Favorite: The lyrical, rhythmic text and calming message make it an ideal bedtime story.

Emotional Resonance for Adults: While meant for children, the book often brings parents and caregivers to tears. It perfectly captures the overwhelming love and awe they feel for their child.

Builds Self-Worth: The repeated affirmation of the child's specialness is a powerful tool for building early self-esteem.

Common Uses and Traditions
Reading Aloud: Its poetic nature makes it perfect for reading aloud.

Personalization: Many families write a personal note on the inside cover, detailing the actual night their child was born.

Classroom Tool: Preschool teachers sometimes use it to talk about how every student is special and unique.

Similar Books
If you love "On the Night You Were Born," you might also enjoy:

"The Wonderful Things You Will Be" by Emily Winfield Martin

"I'd Know You Anywhere, My Love" by Nancy Tillman

"You Are My I Love You" by Maryann Cusimano Love

"Guess How Much I Love You" by Sam McBratney

In summary, "On the Night You Were Born" is more than just a book; it's a tender ritual of love. It assures a child of their priceless place in the world and in the hearts of those who love them, making it a timeless treasure on any child's bookshelf.

video_title: Scribble Stones (encourages creativity, connection, & compassion, inspiring children) #kids #stories
description:
Scribble Stones is a charming and heartfelt children's picture book written and illustrated by Diane Alber. It serves as a stand-alone sequel to her very popular book, I'm NOT Just a Scribble. The story continues to promote themes of kindness, creativity, inclusion, and finding purpose.

The book is known for its simple yet powerful message and its interactive element, as it often comes with a small stone and encourages children to create their own "scribble stone" art.

The Story
The story begins with a happy little stone who thinks his life is perfect. He sits on a large pile of stones, doing what he believes he was meant to do: absolutely nothing. He is content.

However, his world is turned upside down when he is chosen, taken from his pile, and placed on a desk. He soon discovers he is not there to do nothing—he is there to be a paperweight. This is not the purpose he had imagined for himself, and he becomes very unhappy.

Feeling useless and dejected, he is eventually tossed aside into a dark drawer. There, he meets two other discarded items: a scribble and a stack of sticky notes.

Instead of staying sad, they decide to work together. The scribble draws a friendly, smiling face on the stone, completely transforming him. This simple act of creativity and friendship gives the stone a new lease on life. He is no longer just a paperweight; he is now a Scribble Stone!

Inspired and full of joy, the new friends decide to pay it forward. They work together to create more smiling Scribble Stones. The stone's new purpose becomes clear: to spread happiness and kindness to others.

The book ends by challenging the reader: "What will you do?" This directly invites the child to become part of the story and create their own acts of kindness.

Key Themes
Purpose and Identity: The stone learns that his value isn't fixed; he can redefine his purpose and become something wonderful.

Friendship and Teamwork: The stone couldn't have transformed on his own. It took the help of Scribble and the sticky notes to discover his potential.

Kindness and Spreading Joy: The core message is that one small act of creativity and kindness can create a ripple effect, making the world a happier place.

Creativity and Art: The book celebrates art as a powerful tool for expression and connection.

The "Scribble Stone" Project & Interactive Element
This is what makes the book truly special. Many editions of the book come with a small, smooth, white stone tucked into a pocket inside the front cover.

The Challenge: The story inspires children to create their own Scribble Stone by drawing a friendly face or a design on the provided stone.

The Mission: After creating their stone, the child is encouraged to give it to someone to brighten their day, hide it for someone to find, or keep it as a reminder to spread kindness.

This interactive project has sparked a massive movement, with families, schools, and libraries creating and hiding Scribble Stones in their communities.

The Author-Illustrator: Diane Alber
Diane Alber is a best-selling author and illustrator known for her relatable characters and social-emotional learning (SEL) themes. Her books, including the SPOT series (about emotions) and I'm NOT Just a Scribble, are designed to help children navigate their feelings and the world around them. She often uses simple, expressive drawings that are appealing and accessible to young children.

Who is it For?
The book is ideally suited for children ages 3-8. It's a perfect read-aloud for:

Parents and caregivers wanting to teach lessons about empathy and kindness.

Teachers looking for a story to support SEL curricula, art projects, or anti-bullying initiatives.

Art teachers and librarians seeking a fun, engaging activity for storytime.

In summary, Scribble Stones is more than just a book; it's an experience that encourages creativity, connection, and compassion, inspiring children to make their world a brighter place, one stone at a time.

The Paper Dolphin

Suddenly one day,
A dolphin did appear,
It was blue and smiley,
And happy to be here.

It could fit into small spaces,
It was practical like that,
It visited many places,
Voila! Now it has a hat.

Could dance and soar,

That made him wonder in awe.

Perhaps it was time to visit the shore.

First snacks, then play,
The water was nearly in reach.

It was finally time to swim.

What a wonderful thing.

There was so much to see,
A girl, a bird,
Then the bottom of the sea.

That very same afternoon, a new dolphin was born,
It was pink and glittery,
Something like a dolphin unicorn.

The new dolphin asked, “Can I swim?”
Absolutely not,
We won’t even try.
This dolphin unicorn can only fly.

The End.

video_title: Mango, Abuela, and Me (celebrates family, love, patience) Kids & Family Picture Book | Read Aloud
description:
“Mango, Abuela, and Me” is a heartwarming children’s picture book written by Meg Medina and beautifully illustrated by Angela Dominguez. The story revolves around the relationship between a young girl named Mia and her abuela (grandmother) who comes to live with her family. Here’s a glimpse into this touching tale:

The Premise:
Mia’s grandmother leaves her sunny home with parrots and palm trees to join Mia and her parents in the city. However, there’s a language barrier—Abuela doesn’t speak English, and Mia’s Spanish isn’t quite enough to bridge the gap.
Despite their communication challenges, Mia and Abuela embark on a journey to understand each other, learn about their shared past, and create new memories.
The Struggle:
While Mia’s parents are at work during the winter days, Abuela eagerly awaits Mia’s return from school.
Their mouths are as empty as their bread baskets—neither can express themselves fully. Mia longs to share her achievements and stories, while Abuela’s English is too limited to narrate tales of her past and her late husband, Abuelo.
The Word-Card Game:
One day, Mia decides to play a game with Abuela. She pretends to be her teacher, Miss Wilson, and points to objects, teaching Abuela English words.
Abuela responds in Spanish, and they roll out dough for meat pies together. Through this playful interaction, they begin to understand each other better.
Mango, the Bird:
Mia’s pet bird, Mango, becomes a bridge between them. Abuela teaches Mango Spanish phrases, and Mia translates them into English.
Mango’s chirps and songs become a shared language, connecting three generations.
Love and Patience:
Despite the challenges, Mia and Abuela’s bond grows stronger. They find ways to communicate, share memories, and create their own unique language.
Abuela’s love and warmth envelop Mia, and the city apartment feels a little more like home.
This beautifully crafted book celebrates family, love, and the resilience of the human spirit. It reminds us that even when words fail, gestures, shared moments, and the language of the heart can bridge any divide. 📚❤️(AI generated).

"Old Mother Goose" The figure of Mother Goose is the imaginary author of a collection of French fairy tales and later of English nursery rhymes. As a character, she appeared in a song, the first stanza of which often functions now as a nursery rhyme.This, however, was dependent on a Christmas pantomime, a successor to which is still performed in the United Kingdom.
The term's appearance in English dates back to the early 18th century, when Charles Perrault's fairy tale collection, Contes de ma Mère l'Oye, was first translated into English as Tales of My Mother Goose. Later a compilation of English nursery rhymes, titled Mother Goose's Melody, or, Sonnets for the Cradle, helped perpetuate the name both in Britain and the United States.

video_title: Pete the Cat 3 Books for Toddler-Kindergarten | Kids & Family Together Story Time Read Aloud
description:
Pete the Cat is a beloved character in children’s literature. Created by author James Dean.
1. Pete the Cat is back with another groovy adventure! In “Pete the Cat and the Itsy Bitsy Spider”, Pete puts his own cool twist on the classic children’s song. Here’s what you need to know:
The itsy bitsy spider climbs up the water spout, but when the rain comes down, it faces a challenge.
Pete and his friends step in to help out! They know just what to do to assist the struggling spider.
Young readers will laugh, sing along, and enjoy this delightful adaptation.
The book is filled with James Dean’s signature illustrations and catchy rhymes. It’s perfect for kids aged 2 to 4 years and makes for a fun read-aloud experience. So grab your copy, join Pete, and let’s rock out with the itsy bitsy spider! 🕷️.
2. Pete the Cat is always up for a groovy adventure! In his book “Pete the Cat: Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star,” he puts his own cool spin on the classic bedtime song. Here’s what you need to know:
Pete takes the familiar tune of “Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star” and rocks out to it before bedtime.
Whether you’re a new Pete the Cat fan or have been grooving with him for a while, you’ll love singing along to this delightful adaptation.
The book is available in sturdy board book format, making it perfect for little hands to explore.
James Dean’s signature illustrations and catchy rhymes make this book a hit with kids aged 2 to 5 years. So grab your copy, join Pete, and let the stars twinkle as you sing along! 🌟🎶.
3. “Pete the Cat: Old MacDonald Had a Farm” is a groovy rendition of the classic favorite children’s song. Created by James Dean and Kimberly Dean, this delightful picture book features our cool cat Pete as he sings along to the familiar tune of “Old MacDonald Had a Farm.” Here are the details:
Title: Pete the Cat: Old MacDonald Had a Farm
Author & Illustrator: James Dean
Publication Date: February 18, 2014

video_title: The Bee Tree (Community &Togetherness) #toddlers #kindergarten #kidsbooks #school #education #kids
description:
The Bee Tree is a heartwarming, semi-autobiographical picture book written and illustrated by Patricia Polacco. Published in 1993, it is a classic story that celebrates the joy of reading, the importance of intergenerational relationships, and the sweet rewards of a shared adventure.

Plot Summary
The story is set in rural Michigan and is narrated by a young girl named Mary Ellen. Feeling restless and bored with her reading lesson, she complains to her grandfather that she’d rather be outside playing.

Instead of scolding her, her grandfather proposes an exciting alternative: they will go out to find a bee tree. He explains that where there are bees, there is honey, and "the sweetest rewards come from the greatest effort."

Grandfather grabs a jar from the kitchen, and they catch a single bee. They tie a thread to the jar with a piece of cloth, release the bee, and follow it as it flies back to its hive to deliver its nectar. This begins a wild, impromptu chase through the countryside.

Their simple pursuit quickly turns into a community event. They are joined by a colorful cast of neighbors and friends one by one—each dropping what they are doing to join the thrilling chase. They run through fields, past grazing cows, and through a town, causing a delightful ruckus.

Finally, the bee leads them to a hollow tree teeming with bees. Grandfather, an experienced beekeeper, knows just what to do. He smokes the bees to calm them and collects the golden honey.

The adventure culminates in a large, joyful picnic under the tree. Everyone shares the delicious honey on fresh bread, laughing and telling stories. At the end of the day, Mary Ellen and her grandfather sit together. He puts a dab of honey on her book and tells her, “There is such sweetness inside of that book too!” He compares the pursuit of knowledge to their chase for the bee tree: it requires patience and effort, but the reward is just as sweet.

Mary Ellen, having experienced the thrill of the journey and the sweetness of the reward, is finally eager to discover the "sweetness" waiting for her inside her book.

Key Themes
The Joy and Reward of Reading: This is the central theme. The entire bee tree chase is an elaborate metaphor for the adventure of learning. Grandfather teaches Mary Ellen that the effort of reading is well worth it for the "sweet" knowledge and stories one finds inside books.

Intergenerational Wisdom: The story highlights the special bond between a grandparent and grandchild. Grandfather doesn't force Mary Ellen to read; he uses his wisdom, patience, and creativity to inspire her love for learning through experience.

Community and Togetherness: The spontaneous way the community joins the chase shows the importance of neighbors and shared experiences. The reward (the honey) is not kept for themselves but is enjoyed by everyone, strengthening community bonds.

The Value of Effort and Patience: The message is clear: the best things in life require work and perseverance. The easy path (staying home) is boring, while the challenging path (the chase) is exciting and ultimately far more rewarding.

Patricia Polacco's Signature Style
Artwork: Polacco’s illustrations are vibrant and energetic. She uses bold lines and watercolors to bring the chaotic, joyful chase to life. The characters' expressions are full of emotion and movement.

Storytelling: The story is based on her own family tales, a hallmark of her work. It feels personal and authentic.

Characters: The characters are warm, expressive, and often drawn from her own heritage and childhood memories.

Why It's a Beloved Classic
Relatable Problem: Every child (and adult) has felt bored or frustrated with a difficult task. Mary Ellen's initial reluctance is instantly relatable.

The Perfect Metaphor: The bee tree metaphor is simple, powerful, and deliciously tangible for a child. Comparing knowledge to honey is a brilliant way to make an abstract concept appealing.

Sense of Adventure: The wild, carefree chase across the countryside is pure fun and captures the imagination.

Warmth and Joy: The book radiates warmth, from the loving relationship between Mary Ellen and her grandfather to the inclusive community picnic at the end.

video_title: François Clemmons Reflects on Mister Rogers' Neighborhood
description:
In February 1968, the children’s television program “Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood” debuted nationally.

Besides its eponymous creator, the show also featured a cast of characters from Mister Rogers’ make-believe world (King Friday XIII, Daniel Striped Tiger, and Bob Dog), and his “real” world (Mr. and Mrs. McFeely, Lady Aberlin, and Handyman Negri).

François Clemmons was cast in the “real” world as Officer Clemmons.

Fred Rogers met François in 1968 after hearing him sing in a Pittsburgh-area church they both attended. He was so impressed with his voice that he asked him to join the show. At the time, François was a graduate student working on getting his singing career going and was reluctant to accept Fred’s offer. But after realizing he would get paid to appear on the show—enabling him to afford his rent—François accepted, becoming the first African American actor to have a recurring role on a children’s television series.

For 25 years François appeared on the show while maintaining a separate career as a professional singer. In 1973, his performance with the Cleveland Orchestra earned him a Grammy Award and his love of spiritual music later led him to found the Harlem Spiritual Ensemble. He also spent 16 years as an artist-in-residence at Middlebury College in Vermont until his retirement in 2013.

François came to StoryCorps with his friend, Karl Lindholm (pictured together above), to discuss how he became the friendly singing Officer Clemmons, and his relationship with the man known to children as Mister Rogers.

video_title: Wild Fibonacci: Nature's Secret Code Revealed
description:
Wild Fibonacci: Nature's Secret Code Revealed by Joy N. Hulme, illustrated by Carol Schwartz. Read by Riko.

1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34. . . Look carefully. Do you see the pattern? Each number above is the sum of the two numbers before it. Though most of us are unfamiliar with it, this numerical series, called the Fibonacci sequence, is part of a code that can be found everywhere in nature. Count the petals on a flower or the peas in a peapod. The numbers are all part of the Fibonacci sequence. In Wild Fibonacci, readers will discover this mysterious code in a special shape called an equiangular spiral. Why so special? It mysteriously appears in the natural world: a sundial shell curves to fit the spiral. So does a parrot's beak. . . a hawk's talon. . . a ram's horn. . . even our own human teeth! Joy Hulme provides a clear and accessible introduction to the Fibonacci sequence and its presence in the animal world.

video_title: Little Blue Truck - Kids Read Aloud Audiobook
description:
Beep! Beep! Meet Blue! Filled with truck sounds and animal noises, Little Blue Truck is a rollicking homage to the power of friendship and the rewards of helping others.
   A muddy country road is no match for this little pick-up—that is, until he gets stuck while pushing a dump truck out of the muck.  Luckily, Blue has made a pack of farm animal friends along his route. And they're willing to do whatever it takes to get their pal back on the road.
   Little Blue Truck is a joyful cacophony of animal and truck sounds that will have youngsters beeping and quacking—and begging for one more go-round! 
   In this heartwarming story, readers see that it pays to be kind to our animal friends. If we show a friendly respect to others, we’re more likely to get help when we’re, say, stuck in the muck in a truck!

description:
In this simple, touching picture book about the healing power of a loving community, a girl's grandpa and her neighbors help her grow an olive tree in a war-torn land. Thanks to author Hazar Elbayya for stopping by!

About MY OLIVE TREE

Salam’s grandpa says that olive trees are strong and that their roots run deep in their Palestinian land. They connect everyone–from the farmer who presses the olives into oil to the baker who uses the oil in his taboon.

Salam plants her own seed and is eager to see it grow. She waits… she waters… she asks the seed to hurry… until finally…a sprout! But one day soldiers come and destroy everything in their path…including Salam’s new olive tree. Salam is crushed–though she doesn’t have to worry. Her grandpa gathers their neighbors and, together, they plant olive trees as far as the eye can see. 

With spare, sensitive prose and gentle illustrations, debut author-illustrator Hazar Elbayya delivers a powerful story about the beauty of the olive tree and the importance of community in the face of hardship.

“The Little Old Lady Who Was Not Afraid of Anything” is a delightful Halloween picture book written by Linda D. Williams and illustrated by Megan Lloyd. Originally published in 1998, this timeless tale invites readers into a world where courage and cleverness triumph over fear.

Here’s a glimpse into the story:

Once upon a time, there was a little old lady who was not afraid of anything! But one autumn night, while walking in the woods, the little old lady heard…

Clomp, clomp (heavy footsteps)
Shake, shake (rustling clothes)
Clap, clap (clapping hands)
These spooky sounds followed her home from the forest. But the little old lady remained unafraid. Instead, she hatched a clever plan. She invited each item—a pair of pants, a shirt, gloves, a hat, and even a pumpkin head—into her cozy cottage. There, she gave them a new purpose: they became her scarecrow in the garden!

With bouncy refrains and classic art, this Halloween story is perfect for reading aloud. Whether you’re curled up at home or sharing it in a classroom or library setting, both you and the kids will be enchanted by the little old lady’s fearless attitude and her ingenious solution to the lively, spooky items that once followed her. description:
“Stumpkin” by Lucy Ruth Cummins is a heartwarming picture book that celebrates uniqueness, friendship, and the magic of Halloween. Let me share a brief summary of this delightful tale:

Stumpkin, the most handsome pumpkin on the block, is as orange as a traffic cone and twice as round as a basketball. He has no bad side and seems like the perfect choice for a Halloween jack-o’-lantern.
However, there’s a catch: Stumpkin has a stump instead of a stem. Unfortunately, no one seems to want a stemless jack-o’-lantern for their window.
As Halloween night approaches, Stumpkin watches his fellow pumpkins find homes, but he remains unchosen. Will anyone give Stumpkin the chance to shine and become the jack-o’-lantern he dreams of being?
This heartwarming story teaches children about acceptance, empathy, and the beauty of being true to oneself. Stumpkin’s journey reminds us that sometimes what makes us different is what makes us special. 🎃
Remember, even a stemless pumpkin can light up the night with its unique glow!

Nancy White Carlstrom is the author of more than fifty books for children, including nine other titles in the Jesse Bear series, Who Said Boo?, and Wild Wild Sunflower Child Anna. Ms. Carlstrom lives in Fairbanks, Alaska, with her husband, David, and their two son, Jesse and Josh. And while the olive too far away for frequent visits with their family, they enjoy traveling to see their family as often as possible.

Bruce Degen has illustrated all the Jesse Bear books. He is the author and illustrator of Jamberry, and the illustrator of the acclaimed Magic School Bus series. He has taught courses on art and the writing and illustrating of children's books to children and adults. Mr. Degen, his wife, and their two sons, Benjamin and Alexander, live in Connecticut in a renovated farmhouse with ducks on the pond, bats in the barn, and a family tree that Jesse Bear himself would love to climb.

Experience the touching story of 'Bear Feels Sad' by Karma Wilson, a beautiful kids-book perfect for storytime! This heartwarming readaloud explores emotions and friendship. This story is read by Cody Daniel, Corinth Librarian. Join us for this delightful reading and embark on a journey of understanding and empathy.✨

In 'Bear Feels Sad,' we follow Bear as he experiences a range of emotions, feeling down and not quite himself. His loyal friends try to cheer him up, showing how true companionship can help overcome difficult feelings. This lovely children's book teaches young readers about empathy, coping with sadness, and the power of friendship. It’s an essential read for anyone exploring feelings and support, making it an excellent addition to any home or classroom library. Enjoy this readalong with your little ones! 🐻📚

video_title: Children's Story Read Aloud The Snow Queen
description:
Children's Story Read Aloud The Snow Queen

The walls of the palace were driven snow. The windows and doors were the knife-edged wind. There were more than a hundred halls, shaped as the snow had drifted, and the largest of these extended for many a mile. All were lighted by the flare of the Northern Lights. All of the halls were so immense and so empty, so brilliant and so glacial! There was never a touch of gaiety in them; never so much as a little dance for the polar bears, at which the storm blast could have served for music, and the polar bears could have waddled about on their hind legs to show off their best manners. There was never a little party with such games as blind-bear's buff or hide the paw-kerchief for the cubs, nor even a little afternoon coffee over which the white fox vixens could gossip. Empty, vast, and frigid were the Snow Queen's halls. The Northern Lights flared with such regularity that you could time exactly when they would be at the highest and lowest. In the middle of the vast, empty hall of snow was a frozen lake. It was cracked into a thousand pieces, but each piece was shaped so exactly like the others that it seemed a work of wonderful craftsmanship. The Snow Queen sat in the exact center of it when she was at home, and she spoke of this as sitting on her "Mirror of Reason." She said this mirror was the only one of its kind, and the best thing in all the world.

Little Kay was blue, yes, almost black, with the cold. But he did not feel it, because the Snow Queen had kissed away his icy tremblings, and his heart itself had almost turned to ice.

He was shifting some sharp, flat pieces of ice to and fro, trying to fit them into every possible pattern, for he wanted to make something with them. It was like the Chinese puzzle game that we play at home, juggling little flat pieces of wood about into special designs. Kay was cleverly arranging his pieces in the game of ice-cold reason. To him the patterns were highly remarkable and of the utmost importance, for the chip of glass in his eye made him see them that way. He arranged his pieces to spell out many words; but he could never find the way to make the one word he was so eager to form. The word was "Eternity." The Snow Queen had said to him, "If you can puzzle that out you shall be your own master, and I'll give you the whole world and a new pair of skates." But he could not puzzle it out.

"Now I am going to make a flying trip to the warm countries," the Snow Queen told him. "I want to go and take a look into the black caldrons." She meant the volcanos of Etna and Vesuvius. "I must whiten them up a bit. They need it, and it will be such a relief after all those yellow lemons and purple grapes."

And away she flew. Kay sat all alone in that endless, empty, frigid hall, and puzzled over the pieces of ice until he almost cracked his skull. He sat so stiff and still that one might have thought he was frozen to death.

All of a sudden, little Gerda walked up to the palace through the great gate which was a knife-edged wind. But Gerda said her evening prayer. The wind was lulled to rest, and the little girl came on into the vast, cold, empty hall. Then she saw Kay. She recognized him at once, and ran to throw her arms around him. She held him close and cried, "Kay, dearest little Kay! I've found you at last!"

But he sat still, and stiff, and cold. Gerda shed hot tears, and when they fell upon him they went straight to his heart. They melted the lump of ice and burned away the splinter of glass in it. He looked up at her, and she sang:

"Where roses bloom so sweetly in the vale,
There shall you find the Christ Child, without fail."
Kay burst into tears. He cried so freely that the little piece of glass in his eye was washed right out. "Gerda!" He knew her, and cried out in his happiness, "My sweet little Gerda, where have you been so long? And where have I been?" He looked around him and said, "How cold it is here! How enormous and empty!" He held fast to Gerda, who laughed until happy tears rolled down her cheeks. Their bliss was so heavenly that even the bits of glass danced about them and shared in their happiness. When the pieces grew tired, they dropped into a pattern which made the very word that the Snow Queen had told Kay he must find before he became his own master and received the whole world and a new pair of skates.

"The Potty Books for Boys" is a popular and effective genre of children's books designed to make the potty training journey fun, relatable, and successful.

Here is a comprehensive guide to this genre, including why they work, what to look for, and a list of highly recommended titles.

Why Potty Training Books Are Effective for Boys
Normalization: They show that every child goes through this process, making it feel like a normal part of growing up.

Modeling Behavior: Boys can see characters (both human and animal) successfully using the potty, which provides a clear model to imitate.

Boy-Specific Tips: Many books address standing vs. sitting, aim, and other boy-specific nuances that general books might skip.

Reduces Anxiety: They can tackle common fears (fear of flushing, falling in, loud noises) in a gentle, reassuring way.

Engagement & Fun: Bright pictures, engaging stories, and fun sounds ("Tinkle, tinkle, toot!") make the process more like a game than a chore.

video_title: If You Give a Pig a Pancake funny & clever() #educational #toddlers #kindergarten #kidsbooks #story
description:
"If You Give a Pig a Pancake" is a beloved modern classic in children's literature. Here's a detailed breakdown of the book.

Overview
Title: If You Give a Pig a Pancake

Author: Laura Numeroff

Illustrator: Felicia Bond

Publication Date: 1998

Series: Part of the hugely popular "If You Give..." series, which includes If You Give a Mouse a Cookie and If You Give a Moose a Muffin.

The Story in a Nutshell
The story follows a familiar and hilarious circular pattern. A little girl is confronted by an enthusiastic, demanding pig who wants a pancake. Each action by the little girl leads directly to a new, often extravagant, request from the pig, creating a chaotic and comical chain of events.

The plot is a perfect example of a cause-and-effect story that highlights the boundless energy and ever-shifting focus of a young child.

The Chain of Events (Spoiler Alert!)
The sequence of requests goes something like this:

If you give a pig a pancake, she'll want some syrup to go with it.

She'll get all sticky, so she'll want a bath.

In the bath, she'll ask for bubbles.

The bubbles will remind her of the circus, so she'll want to tap dance.

To tap dance, she'll need a costume.

When she's trying on the costume, she'll ask for rubber boots.

She'll want to wear her backpack with the boots.

She'll look in the backpack and find doll clothes, which will make her want to send a letter.

To send a letter, she'll need tape.

When she sees the sticky tape, it will remind her of the syrup...

...which will remind her that she wants another pancake!

The story ends exactly where it began, ready to start the cycle all over again.

Themes and Why Kids Love It
Cause and Effect: The book is a fantastic, fun way to teach young children about logical sequences and consequences.

Predictability and Pattern: The circular story is predictable in its pattern, which gives young readers a sense of mastery and comfort. They love anticipating what the pig will ask for next.

Humor and Exaggeration: The pig's requests are increasingly silly and over-the-top, which children find utterly hilarious.

Relatability: The pig's boundless energy, messiness, and rapidly changing desires are very familiar to both children and parents. It's a gentle, funny mirror of a preschooler's day.

The Patient Caregiver: The little girl in the story is endlessly patient and accommodating, much like a parent or older sibling, which adds a layer of warmth and comfort to the chaos.

Educational Value
Language Development: The repetitive and rhythmic text is excellent for building vocabulary and narrative skills.

Cognitive Skills: It encourages prediction, memory (remembering the sequence), and understanding of logical progression.

Sequencing Activities: Teachers and parents often use this book for activities where children can put the events in order using pictures or props.

About the Illustrations
Felicia Bond's illustrations are a key part of the book's charm. They are:

Expressive: The pig's emotions—excitement, sadness, joy—are vividly drawn and easy for children to read.

Detailed: The pictures are filled with fun little details that aren't mentioned in the text, encouraging children to spend time on each page exploring.

Chaotic and Fun: They perfectly capture the escalating mess and energy of the pig's demands.

Overall
If You Give a Pig a Pancake is a delightful, funny, and clever book that has earned its place on countless bookshelves. Its perfect blend of a simple, predictable structure with chaotic, relatable humor makes it a surefire hit for read-aloud sessions with children aged 3-7.

In short: It's a story about how one small, kind act (giving a pancake) can lead to a wonderfully chaotic and fun-filled adventure.

Eventually, the scribble becomes the catalyst for a new, unexpected story that’s even better than the original.

video_title: The Very Impatient Caterpillar (teaches kids about waiting & transformation) #kids #reading #story
description:
The Very Impatient Caterpillar is a humorous and engaging children's picture book written and illustrated by Ross Burach. It was published in 2019 and quickly became a favorite among kids and parents for its funny take on the classic caterpillar-to-butterfly transformation.

Plot Summary:
The story follows an overly excited and very impatient caterpillar who learns about metamorphosis and decides he wants to become a butterfly—RIGHT NOW!

When the other caterpillars explain that he must first go into his chrysalis and wait, he struggles with the concept of patience. Throughout the book, he keeps asking, "Am I a butterfly yet?!" while misunderstanding the process (at one point, he thinks he’s turning into a "butter-chicken").

Finally, after some comedic frustration, he emerges as a beautiful butterfly—only to realize that now he must wait for his wings to dry!

Themes & Why Kids Love It:
Patience & Growth – The book playfully teaches kids about waiting and transformation.

Humor – The caterpillar’s over-the-top impatience and silly questions make kids laugh.

Science Connection – Introduces metamorphosis in a fun, accessible way.

Sequels & Series:
Ross Burach expanded this into a series, including:

The Little Butterfly That Could (2021) – About a butterfly struggling with migration.

Goodnight, Butterfly (2022) – A bedtime story with the same characters.

Perfect For:
Ages 3–7

Parents/teachers discussing life cycles, patience, or humor in storytelling.

description:
Title: Perfect Square
Author: Michael Hall  

Theme:
Perfect Square explores themes of resilience, adaptability, and transformation. It emphasizes how challenges and changes can lead to new opportunities and beauty, even when things don’t go as planned. The story encourages readers to embrace imperfections and find creativity in adversity.

Summary:
The book follows a happy, perfect square—a square that is content with its symmetry and perfection. Each day of the week, the square undergoes a transformation: it is cut, torn, crumpled, or shattered. At first, these changes seem to destroy its perfection, but the square creatively adapts, reshaping itself into something new and beautiful, like a fountain, mountain, or river. By the end of the week, the square is no longer "perfect," but it discovers that it can still find joy and purpose in its new forms.

 Lessons:
1. **Resilience:** The square demonstrates how to bounce back from challenges and find new ways to thrive.  
2. **Adaptability:** It shows that change, though sometimes difficult, can lead to unexpected and beautiful outcomes.  
3. **Creativity:** The square uses its imagination to transform setbacks into opportunities.  
4. **Embracing Imperfection:** The story teaches that perfection isn’t necessary for happiness or fulfillment.  
5. **Growth Through Adversity:** The square’s journey illustrates how struggles can lead to personal growth and new perspectives.  

*Perfect Square* is a visually engaging and thought-provoking picture book that resonates with both children and adults, reminding us that life’s imperfections can be sources of creativity and joy.

video_title: Honey Bee Busy Day (Simple, Educational Story) #toddlers #kindergarten #kidsbooks #school #library
description:
"Honey Bee Busy Day" by Richard Fowler is a classic and beloved children's lift-the-flap book.

Here is a detailed overview of the book:

"Honey Bee's Busy Day" by Richard Fowler
Overview:
"Honey Bee's Busy Day" is an interactive board book designed for very young children, typically toddlers and preschoolers. First published in the 1990s, it has remained a popular choice for its engaging, hands-on approach to storytelling and learning.

The book follows a friendly honey bee through a day of activities, from leaving the hive in the morning to returning at night. The central interactive feature is a large, yellow, bee-shaped finger puppet that is attached to the spine of the book and pokes through a hole on every page. This allows the child (or the adult reader) to physically "fly" the bee through each scene as the story is read.

Key Features:
The Finger Puppet Bee: This is the book's standout feature. The sturdy puppet is sewn into the binding, making it durable enough to withstand enthusiastic little hands. Children can wiggle the bee, make it "fly" to different flowers, and interact with the illustrations on each page.

Lift-the-Flap Elements: True to Richard Fowler's style, the book is filled with sturdy flaps for children to lift. These flaps reveal hidden surprises, additional characters, or parts of the story, encouraging exploration and fine motor skill development.

For example, a flap on a flower might lift to reveal a drop of nectar, or a leaf might hide another insect.

Simple, Educational Story: The narrative is straightforward and rhythmic, perfect for short attention spans. It seamlessly incorporates basic concepts about nature and a bee's role in it:

Pollination: The bee collects pollen and nectar from different flowers.

Colors and Counting: The bee visits flowers of various colors (e.g., red poppies, blue bluebells), introducing color names. The act of visiting multiple flowers introduces a counting element.

The Life Cycle: The bee returns to the hive, where the honey is stored, touching on how honey is made.

Bright and Friendly Illustrations: Richard Fowler's artwork is cheerful, clear, and cartoonish, not realistic. The characters, including the bee and other insects, have smiling, friendly faces, making the natural world seem inviting and unthreatening to young children.

Why It's a Favorite:
Interactive and Engaging: The combination of puppet and flaps creates a highly immersive reading experience. It transforms storytime from a passive activity into an active, participatory one.

Durable Construction: As a board book with thick pages and sturdy flaps, it is built to last through multiple readings and rough handling.

Educational Value: It introduces toddlers to fundamental concepts of nature, science, and cause-and-effect in a very fun and accessible way.

Perfect for Read-Aloud: The interactive elements make it a fantastic book for bonding during read-aloud sessions. Parents can guide the child's hand with the bee or let them operate the puppet themselves.

In summary, "Honey Bee's Busy Day" is a quintessential example of a well-designed interactive children's book. Richard Fowler successfully combines a simple story about nature with tactile elements that captivate young readers, making learning about bees a delightful and "busy" adventure.

In this book from the critically acclaimed, multimillion-copy best-selling Little People, BIG DREAMS series, discover the incredible life of Vanessa Nakate, the Ugandan climate-justice activist.  

As a kid, when little Vanessa heard about climate change, she thought it was something that happened on the other side of the world. As an adult, she saw how droughts in her own country led to crop failure that left families hungry. Inspired by other activists, Vanessa took a stand and began campaigning to save the Congolian rain forests. Soon, she was invited to take her campaign around the world.

In 2020, Vanessa participated in an important summit about climate change. But when she was cropped out of a photograph featuring other climate-change activists, it felt like not just her contribution to the movement had been erased, but that the needs of a whole continent had been disregarded.

It was a moment that shocked the world, but it spurred Vanessa on to raise her voice louder and to fight harder for climate justice for Africans. Today, she continues to be a leader in the climate-change movement and a voice of her generation.

About MI CIUDAD SINGS

After experiencing a devastating earthquake, the spirit of a charming and vibrant Mexican neighborhood might be shaken, but it cannot be broken.

As a little girl and her dog embark on their daily walk through the city, they skip and spin to the familiar sounds of revving cars, clanking bikes, friendly barks, and whistling camote carts. But what they aren’t expecting to hear is the terrifying sound of a rumbling earthquake…and then…silence.
 
With captivating text and lively, beautiful illustrations, this heartwarming story leaves readers with the message that they can choose to be strong and brave even when they are scared, and can still find joy and hope in the midst of sadness.

******

About MI CIUDAD CANTA
Después de vivir un temblor devastador, el espíritu de los vecinos en esta dinámica zona de la ciudad Mexicana se sacude, pero no se rompe.
 

Una pequeña niña y su perro se aventuran en su caminata diaria por la ciudad; brincan y giran con el sonido familiar de coches acelerando, de bicicletas rechinando, de amigables ladridos, y de los silbidos del carrito de camotes. Pero lo que no esperan es escuchar el escalofriante estruendo de un temblor… y después…silencio.
 
Con un texto cautivador y hermosas ilustraciones, esta cálida y reconfortante historia permite a los lectores reconocer que se puede escoger ser valientes y fuertes aún cuando se tiene miedo, y encontrar alegría y esperanza en medio de la tristeza.

video_title: PIPPIN PALS are HERO HELPERS! by Donna Marie (Pandemic Theme)
description:
The Covid-19 pandemic has flipped the world on its head and adjusting our lifestyles has been challenging, to say the least, especially for kids. It has also made clear who we should consider true Heroes — those who sacrifice their own safety for the sake of others. The Pippin Pals are Hero Helpers! story highlights these hard pandemic-related issues, “softened” through rhyme, and encompasses the pandemic experience through a child’s eyes, validating their feelings in a tangible way.

To offer a more personalized experience for the readers, the eight Pippin Pals are Hero Helpers! books are not a series, but diverse and inclusive versions of the same story; you choose the version or versions which align with your or a child’s/student’s preferences for the main characters and their families.

The books aid a child’s understanding as to why things have changed, how to adjust to the “new normal,” and reinforce the ways to comply. Through vivid, visual depictions of how germs spread, and the basic “dos and don’ts” that help protect themselves, people they love, and ultimately — heroic workers — they become Hero Helpers! The books feature those essential workers (be sure to check the end papers!), school from home, being social virtually, and the positive aspects of stay-at-home and “stay safe” living, along with a surprise “rainbow of hope” activity.

video_title: Walking Through a World of Aromas By Ariel Andrés Almada
description:
When Annie was born, everything was dark. She could feel the warmth of her mother as she held her in her arms, the smell of her father’s newly washed shirt, and far away, she could hear the twittering of the birds as they slowly woke up to spring. But apart from that, everything else was darkness..

Annie spends her days cooking in an old house with her grandma. Although she can’t see, Annie has the gift of being able to feel our very deepest emotions and to bring them to life with her magical mixtures of cinnamon and saffron. But one day, she meets a person who awakens a boundless affection in her, someone who will introduce her senses to a completely unknown world.

If we set our minds to it, we can all turn what we perceive as weaknesses into strengths.

The possibility of a film sequel has been confirmed and denied many times in recent years by the original cast and crew. Sean Astin told MTV in October 2007 that Goonies 2 "is an absolute certainty ... The writing's on the wall when they're releasing the DVD in such numbers." video_title: The Very Last Leaf (finding courage within) #kids #toddlers #kindergarten #story #books #reading
description:
The Last Leaf is a charming and insightful picture book written by Stef Wade and illustrated by Jennifer Davison. Published in 2020 by Capstone Editions, it tells the story of a worried little leaf named Lance who is facing a universal fear: the unknown.

The book uses the changing seasons as a gentle metaphor for anxiety, courage, and the importance of supporting others, making it a fantastic resource for social-emotional learning.

Plot Summary
Lance is a determined and capable leaf on a giant tree. He takes his job as a leaf very seriously—he soaks up the sun, converts carbon dioxide, and provides shade. He's proud to have earned a spot on the tree's "Top Branch" and is a model leaf.

However, as autumn arrives, Lance's confidence wavers. He watches in alarm as his fellow leaves begin to let go and float to the ground. Lance is not ready. He's filled with anxiety about falling. What if he gets lost? What if the wind tosses him around? What lies below is a complete mystery, and it terrifies him.

He tries everything to hold on. He clings tightly through windstorms and even tries to super-glue himself to his branch (with sap, of course!). His friends, who have already fallen, call up encouragement from the ground below, telling him how fun it is and that the "view is great" down there.

Finally, Lance is the very last leaf on the tree. He feels alone and scared. But with deep breaths and the supportive cheers from his friends, he finds the courage within.

video_title: The Monsters' Monster (choosing sweetness over scares) #kids #toddlers #kindergarten #educational
description:
The Monsters' Monster is a charming and humorous picture book that turns the classic monster trope on its head. The story follows three little monsters—Grouch, Grump, and Little Gloom 'n' Doom—who spend their time arguing over who is the "biggest and baddest" monster of all.

To settle the debate, they decide to build the biggest, baddest monster ever. They gather an assortment of scary items like old screws, rusty nails, and a dusty boot, and use a jolt of lightning to bring their creation to life. The result is a massive, lumbering creature they name the Monster.

However, their creation defies all their expectations. Instead of being fearsome, the Monster's first word is a gentle, grateful, "Dank you!" (Thank you!). He doesn't smash or destroy; he calmly walks through the terrified town, not to scare people, but to get a warm, powdered-sugar jelly donut. He then sits on a hill to peacefully enjoy his treat, sharing it with his three confused creators.

The story ends with the three little monsters, sitting with their giant creation, quietly enjoying the simple, sweet moment and a box of donuts, having learned a new way to be.

Themes and Lessons
1. The True Nature of Kindness and Gratitude:
This is the central theme of the book. The Monster, built to be terrifying, is inherently kind and grateful. His first instinct is to say "thank you," and his greatest desire is something simple and sweet. The book suggests that true strength isn't about being the "biggest and baddest," but about having a gentle and appreciative heart.

2. Appreciating the Simple Joys in Life:
While the little monsters are consumed with negative one-upmanship, the Monster finds pure bliss in a jelly donut, a sunny day, and the company of others. The story is a powerful reminder to slow down and find happiness in life's small, sweet moments.

3. Transformation Through Example (The Power of Influence):
The three little monsters are not punished or scolded into changing their ways. Instead, they are transformed by the Monster's unwavering, gentle example. His calmness and joy are contagious, slowly melting away their grumpiness and showing them a more fulfilling way to live.

4. Letting Go of Expectations:
The little monsters have a very rigid idea of what a monster should be. The real Monster shatters these expectations, teaching them (and the reader) that it's okay when people—or monsters—don't fit into the boxes we create for them. Sometimes, the best things come from unexpected places.

5. The Folly of "Biggest and Baddest" Competitions:
The book is a gentle satire on the pointless nature of trying to out-do others in negativity. The little monsters' constant arguing is shown as silly and unproductive. True contentment, the story argues, comes from cooperation and shared experiences, not from winning a competition of badness.

Lesson for Young Readers
The primary lesson for children is that kindness and gratitude are powerful forces that can bring more happiness than force or anger. It teaches that it's okay to be gentle and to enjoy simple things, and that true strength often lies in being peaceful and thankful. It's a wonderful story about choosing sweetness over scares.

Guess How Much I Love You, written by Sam McBratney and illustrated by Anita Jeram, is a timeless children’s book that has captured the hearts of both young readers and adults alike. Let’s delve into the story behind this beloved picture book:

The Story: The book follows the Nutbrown Hares as they attempt to measure their love for each other. Big Nutbrown Hare’s heartwarming declaration to Little Nutbrown Hare—“I love you right up to the moon—and back”—has become a universal expression of love around the world.
Creators:
Sam McBratney: An author known for his best-selling family classics, Sam McBratney wrote over a hundred books and scripts. His storytelling touched generations of readers, leaving a lasting impact.
Anita Jeram: Born and raised in Portsmouth, Anita Jeram is an illustrator celebrated for her work in children’s storybooks. Her illustrations for Guess How Much I Love You were shortlisted for the 1994 Kurt Maschler Award.
How It All Began: The seed for Guess How Much I Love You was planted during a conversation between Sam McBratney and his editor, Caroline Royds. Sam recalls the moment when his editor suggested he write a picture book. Despite his initial concerns about needing an illustrator, Caroline assured him that they had talented artists who could bring his imagination to life. And so, the heartwarming tale of love, expressed through minimal words and exquisite illustrations, came to be.
This quintessential picture book invites readers to explore the immeasurable depths of love—a sentiment that transcends boundaries and resonates across generations. Whether you’re reading it to a little one or cherishing it yourself, Guess How Much I Love You continues to be a cherished classic that reminds us of the boundless love we share with those we hold dear.

description:
“Measuring Penny” is an exceptional children’s book that seamlessly combines the joy of storytelling with valuable lessons in math and measurement. Authored by Loreen Leedy, this charming tale follows Lisa as she embarks on a quest to measure everything around her, with the help of her beloved dog, Penny 1.

In this delightful picture book, Lisa has an important homework assignment: she must measure something in several different ways. Using both standard units (like inches) and nonstandard units (like paper clips), Lisa explores height, width, length, weight, volume, temperature, and time. But her most exciting measurement adventure involves her dog, Penny:

Penny’s nose measures 1 inch long.
Penny’s tail is the length of 1 dog biscuit.
And Penny’s paw print spans 3 centimeters wide.
As Lisa learns about her dog and the art of measuring, she discovers that math can be both educational and fun. Loreen Leedy’s clear and engaging concept book, delivered with a sense of humor, is certain to win over even the most reluctant mathematician. 📏🐾📚

video_title: 🌺 Proud as a Peacock, Brave as a Lion
description:
Proud as a Peacock, Brave as a Lion by Jane Barclay, illustrated by Renné Benoit. Read by Riko.

Much has been written about war and remembrance, but very little of it has been for young children. As questions come from a young grandchild, his grandpa talks about how, as a very young man, he was as proud as a peacock in uniform, busy as a beaver on his Atlantic crossing, and brave as a lion charging into battle. Soon, the old man's room is filled with an imaginary menagerie as the child thinks about different aspects of wartime. But as he pins medals on his grandpa's blazer and receives his own red poppy in return, the mood becomes more somber.

Outside, the crowd gathered for the veterans' parade grows as quiet as a mouse, while men and women -- old and young -- march past in the rain. A trumpet plays and Grandpa lays a wreath in memory of his lost friend. Just then, the child imagines an elephant in the mist. "Elephants never forget," he whispers to his grandpa. "Then let's be elephants," says the old man, as he wipes water from his eyes and takes his grandson's hand.

Proud as a Peacock, Brave as a Lion has relevance to a growing number of families, as new waves of soldiers leave home.
