Carl Steven ...  Spock - age 9 

Vadia Potenza ...  Spock - age 13 

Stephen Manley ...  Spock - age 17 

► Director: Leonard Nimoy
► Writers: Gene Roddenberry (television series Star Trek), Harve Bennett

☆ Trivia

The Wrath of Khan was a critical and commercial success, and Paramount Pictures quickly prepared for a third Star Trek film. The Wrath of Khan's director, Nicholas Meyer, would not return; he had disagreed with changes made to his film's ending without his consent. Upon seeing The Wrath of Khan, Leonard Nimoy became "excited" about playing Spock again. When asked by Paramount if he wanted to reprise the role for the third feature, Nimoy agreed and told them, "You're damned right, I want to direct that picture!" Studio chief Michael Eisner was reluctant to hire Nimoy because he mistakenly believed that the actor hated Star Trek and had demanded in his contract that Spock be killed. Nimoy was given the job after he persuaded Eisner that this was not the case. Star Trek creator Gene Roddenberry's first reaction to the news was that producer Harve Bennett had "hired a director you can't fire".

Paramount gave Bennett the green light to write Star Trek III the day after The Wrath of Khan opened, the fastest go-ahead the producer had received. He began writing the screenplay, noting that "seventeen other people could have written [it]" after the hints at Spock's resurrection in the previous film. Bennett and Nimoy used the open thread of Spock mind melding with McCoy at the end of The Wrath of Khan as a way to explain Spock's restoration. The idea and name of the Vulcan "katra" came from Bennett's discussions with Nimoy. The actor referred the producer to an episode of the television series, "Amok Time", that suggested to Bennett a high level of "spiritual transference" among the Vulcans. Bennett admitted that the idea of Kirk and company going back to the Genesis planet to recover Kirk's "noble self" stemmed from a poem he read in a Star Trek fan magazine. The film's production acknowledged certain expectations from fans—Nimoy remarked that if Spock had not been resurrected and, instead, "Captain Kirk turn[ed] to the camera and [said] 'Sorry, we didn't find him,' people would throw rocks at the screen." A major issue Bennett wrestled with was how to introduce the story for people who had not seen The Wrath of Khan. Bennett said that his television producer mentality "won out"; he added a "previously in Star Trek ..." film device, and had Kirk narrate a captain's log, describing his feelings and sense of loss. Aware of the story's predictability, Bennett decided to have the USS Enterprise destroyed, and intended this plot element be kept a secret.

description:
Children's story • Audiobook • Read Aloud • Read Along • Online Storytime
Thanksgiving Day Thanks by Laura Malone Elliott
Illustrated by Lynn Munsinger 
Read by Leigh Hood, Northeast Regional Library Branch Manager
Northeast Regional Library • https://nereg.lib.ms.us

Laura Malone Elliott and Lynn Munsinger have created another holiday story about the lovable characters from A String of Hearts.

Perfect for a teacher's classroom or a child's home bookshelf, Thanksgiving Day Thanks tells the story of Sam trying to figure out what he's thankful for.Sam also works on a special project to share at the Thanksgiving feast—his own version of the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade!

Parents and teachers will find inspiration for other Thanksgiving crafts and projects in this charming and funny storybook. A section at the back includes fun Thanksgiving facts.

Full of creativity, humor, and heart, Thanksgiving Day Thanks celebrates friendship, family, and the many other blessings in our lives for which we give thanks.

BOOKLIST - An early education class made up of farm and forest animals discovers the history, traditions, and true meaning of Thanksgiving. Mrs. Wright, the teacher bear, asks the circle of students a question: “What one special thing about the holiday would you give thanks for?” This question gets class members rooting for football, sweet potatoes and marshmallows, and the relatively new ritual of “shopping.” Mrs. Wright asks who knows about the first Thanksgiving, and then sets the class to preparing for its own celebration. The only student stumped by the various questions is Sam the bear—he can think of neither his favorite Thanksgiving ritual nor a Thanksgiving project. But he manages, finally, to come up with a stunning combination of both when he unveils his replica of the Thanksgiving Day Parade balloons. Bolstered by warm watercolor cartoon illustrations, this book is a perfect delivery system for a wealth of knowledge about Thanksgiving, with the story suggesting that family and friends are the main things to be thankful for. Preschool-Grade 2. --Connie Fletcher

video_title: Interrupting Chicken (humor, heart, & clever) #educational #toddlers #kindergarten #kidsbooks #story
description:
Interrupting Chicken is a beloved and hilarious children's book that has become a modern classic. Here's a detailed breakdown.

Summary of Interrupting Chicken
Written and illustrated by David Ezra Stein, the book won a Caldecott Honor in 2011 for its expressive and clever illustrations.

The Plot:
It's bedtime for little red chicken, and Papa is going to read her a story. He agrees, but with one rule: "You are not going to interrupt the story tonight, are you?"
She promises, "I'll be good."

However, as soon as Papa begins a classic fairy tale (like Hansel and Gretel, Little Red Riding Hood, or Chicken Little), the little chicken gets so caught up in the story that she can't help but jump into the page to warn the characters of impending danger, thus ruining the ending every single time.

Hansel and Gretel: Just as they approach the witch's candy house, little chicken bursts in yelling, "DON'T GO IN! SHE'S A WITCH!" So, Hansel and Gretel don't go in, and the story ends abruptly.

Little Red Riding Hood: As Red approaches the bed with the big-eyed wolf, chicken interrupts, "DON'T TALK TO A STRANGER!" And she gets the wolf out of there.

Chicken Little: When the sky starts falling, chicken yells, "THE SKY IS FALLING!" and then tells them it's just an acorn, preventing their panic.

After interrupting three stories, Papa is out of stories and out of patience. Little chicken, still not sleepy, has a brilliant idea: she will tell Papa a story. She creates an original story about "Bedtime for Papa," where Papa Chicken is put to bed by his little chicken. Of course, as she tells her story, Papa begins to interrupt with loud snores—he's fallen fast asleep!

Why It's So Popular with Kids and Parents
It's Relatable: Every parent and child recognizes the bedtime stall tactics. The dynamic is authentic and heartwarming.

Hilarious & Interactive: Kids love the dramatic irony—they know the danger in the fairy tales and love that the little chicken "saves" the day. They eagerly anticipate the next interruption.

Empowering for Kids: The little chicken is the hero of every story. She's not just being naughty; she's being proactive and clever.

The Perfect Twist Ending: The tables turning, with Papa interrupting her story by falling asleep, is a satisfying and sweet conclusion that always gets a laugh.

Beautiful Illustrations: David Ezra Stein's artwork is messy, energetic, and expressive. The shift from the soft, washed-out colors of the "book within a book" fairy tales to the bright, warm colors of the chicken's home is brilliantly done.

Themes and Lessons
The Joy of Reading: The book is a celebration of stories and how engaging they can be.

Parent-Child Bonding: At its core, it's about the special ritual of bedtime stories.

Empathy: The little chicken interrupts out of concern for the characters, showing her empathy.

Creativity: The solution to the problem isn't punishment; it's creativity, as the little chicken makes up her own story.

The Series
The book was so successful that it spawned a series of sequels, including:

Interrupting Chicken and the Elephant of Surprise

Interrupting Chicken: Cookies for Breakfast

Interrupting Chicken: School's First Day

There is also an animated TV series based on the books on Apple TV+.

Sample Read-Aloud Tips (For Parents/Teachers)
Use Different Voices: Give Papa a deep, tired, but loving voice. Use a high, excited, and impulsive voice for the little chicken.

Build Suspense: Pause right before the classic moment in each fairy tale. Let the kids guess what's about to happen and what the little chicken might say.

Get the Kids Involved: Ask them, "Do you think she's going to be able to not interrupt?" or "What should she yell?"

Emphasize the Interruptions: Make the little chicken's interruptions loud, sudden, and full of energy. The contrast is what makes it funny.

Enjoy the Ending: Read Papa's snores with gusto. It's the punchline of the whole book!

In short, Interrupting Chicken is a perfect blend of humor, heart, and clever storytelling that delights readers of all ages.

video_title: The giving tree by shel Silverstein. Children’s poem read aloud in an English accent.
description:
I was reading The Giving Tree to my son for the first time when I realized—with a lump in my throat—that I had become the tree.

The story seems simple: a boy loves a tree, the tree loves the boy. As the boy grows older, he takes—first her apples, then her branches, finally her trunk—until nothing remains but a stump. "And the tree was happy," Silverstein repeats like a lullaby, each iteration cutting deeper.

What shocked me wasn't the tree's self-destruction (though that haunted me). It was recognizing myself in both characters: the child who never thinks to ask "Is this too much?" and the parent who can't imagine saying "No."

Silverstein's deceptively simple drawings—that minimalist apple tree, that faceless boy—become a mirror. We've all been the taker who mistakes love for endless giving. We've all been the giver who confuses sacrifice with worth.

The genius lies in what's not said. Nowhere does the boy say "thank you." Nowhere does the tree say "I matter too." Their dance of devotion and depletion unfolds in stark, aching lines that children understand instinctively and adults feel in their bones.

Critics debate whether it's a beautiful parable of unconditional love or a troubling portrait of codependency. Maybe it's both. What's undeniable is its power—I've seen kindergarteners weep at the stump scene, while CEOs quote it in retirement speeches.

That's the magic of The Giving Tree. It meets you where you are—whether you're the boy climbing branches or the parent with bark worn thin—and asks the quietest, hardest question: "When does giving become losing yourself?"

The giving tree explores themes of selflessness and the complexities of love through the relationship between tree and a boy. 
The story raise this question about giving and taking, highlighting the potential for one sided relationships and the consequences of unconditional love.

video_title: The Karate Kid - Read Along Story Book - DigitalHD - The Empty Hand - Ralph Macchio - Elisabeth Shue
description:
The Karate Kid Read Along Story Book - Empty Hand - based on the film starring Ralph Macchio and Elisabeth Shue redone as a book and cassette tape for the home - Daniel is new in town, and is getting picked on by the local bullies, who all are adept in karate. Determined to stick up for himself, Daniel begins to teach himself karate, only to discover that the caretaker at his apartment seems to be a grand master in karate. Agreeing to teach Daniel, Mr. Miyagi shows Daniel that there is more to karate than violence, and perhaps the best way to solve the problem he has with the bullies is in the All Valley Karate Championship.

The Karate Kid is a 1984 American martial arts drama film produced by Jerry Weintraub, directed by John G. Avildsen, written by Robert Mark Kamen, that stars Ralph Macchio, Pat Morita and Elisabeth Shue. It is an underdog story in the mold of a previous success, the 1976 film Rocky, which Avildsen also directed. The Karate Kid was a commercial success upon release and garnered critical acclaim, earning Morita an Academy Award nomination for Best Supporting Actor. The film became the first in a series, spawning three sequels and a remake in 2010. This book & tape version is based of the karate kid 1984 full movie

► The Cast

Ralph Macchio as Daniel LaRusso
Pat Morita as Kesuke Miyagi
Elisabeth Shue as Ali Mills
William Zabka as Johnny Lawrence
Ron Thomas as Bobby Brown
Rob Garrison as Tommy
Chad McQueen as Dutch
Tony O'Dell as Jimmy
Martin Kove as John Kreese
Randee Heller as Lucille LaRusso
Julie Fields as Susan
Frances Bay as Lady with Dog
William Bassett as Mr Mills

According to the special-edition DVD commentary, the studio originally wanted the role of Mr. Miyagi to be played by Toshiro Mifune, but writer Robert Mark Kamen was opposed to that casting choice feeling that Mifune's interpretation of the character lacked the warmth and humor that the role needed. Mako was also considered for the role of Mr. Miyagi, but was not available due to prior commitments to film Conan the Destroyer, though he would eventually play a similar role in the film Sidekicks. According to Randee Heller, two days after she was cast, Jerry Weintraub informed her that they intended to replace her with Valerie Harper. John G. Avildsen said that after seeing Harper's audition they decided not to replace Heller after all.

► Music

The musical score for The Karate Kid was composed by Bill Conti, a frequent collaborator of director John G. Avildsen since their initial pairing on Rocky (1976). The instrumental score was orchestrated by Jack Eskew and featured pan flute solos by Gheorge Zamfir. On March 12, 2007, Varèse Sarabande released all four Karate Kid scores in a 4-CD box set limited to 2,500 copies worldwide.

A soundtrack album was released in 1984 by Casablanca Records containing many of the contemporary songs featured in the film. Of particular note is Joe Esposito's "You're the Best", featured during the tournament montage near the end of the first film. Originally written for Rocky III, "You're the Best" was rejected by Sylvester Stallone in favor of Survivor's "Eye of the Tiger". Coincidentally, Survivor also performed the main theme ("The Moment of Truth" Music & Lyrics: Bill Conti, Dennis Lambert, Peter Beckett) for The Karate Kid.

Bananarama's 1984 hit song "Cruel Summer" also made its U.S. debut in The Karate Kid but was excluded from the film's soundtrack album. Other songs featured in the film but left off the album include "Please Answer Me" performed by Broken Edge and "The Ride" performed by The Matches.

Track listing for 1984 soundtrack

"The Moment of Truth" (Survivor)
"(Bop Bop) On the Beach" (The Flirts, Jan & Dean)
"No Shelter" (Broken Edge)
"Young Hearts" (Commuter)
"(It Takes) Two to Tango" (Paul Davis)
"Tough Love" (Shandi)
"Rhythm Man" (St. Regis)
"Feel the Night" (Baxter Robertson)
"Desire" (Gang of Four)
"You're the Best" (Joe Esposito)

► Sequels

The original 1984 film had three sequels, and it launched the career of Macchio, who would turn into a teen idol featured on the covers of magazines such as Tiger Beat. It revitalized the acting career of Morita, previously known mostly for his comedic role as Arnold on Happy Days, who was nominated for a Best Supporting Actor Academy Award for his performance as Mr. Miyagi. Morita reprised his role in three sequels.

The Karate Kid Part II: A 1986 sequel in which Daniel accompanies Miyagi on a trip back to Okinawa (Japan), where he is reunited with loved ones, and is challenged by an old adversary.
The Karate Kid Part III: A 1989 sequel in which Kove reappears as Kreese, seeking revenge on Daniel and Miyagi with the help of allies played by Thomas Ian Griffith and Sean Kanan.
The Next Karate Kid: A 1994 revamp sequel in which Hilary Swank appears as Mr. Miyagi's new student, Julie Pierce.
The Karate Kid: A 2010 remake starring Jackie Chan and Jaden Smith

video_title: Back to the Future - Read Along Story Book - Digital HD - Michael J. Fox - Christopher Lloyd - McFly
description:
Back to the Future read along book and tape. It is the year 1985. Marty McFly, a mild-mannered high school student, stopped by Dr. Emmett L. Brown's laboratory to play around with an amplifier. Then he receives a message from Doc that he needs help from him for Doc's latest invention, a time machine made out of a DeLorean sports car that can travel through time instantaneously when it reaches a speed velocity of 88 MPH. Then, Doc was gunned down by Libyan Nationalists, Marty makes an effort to escape from the Lybians by using the time machine. Then Marty accidentally warps himself into 1955. Where he meets both of his parents when they were teenagers, then Marty unintentionally interrupts his parent's first meeting together, he then finds a younger version of Doc and together they try to find a way to get Marty's parents-to-be back together, and to get Marty back to 1985. 

► Cast of the full movie version were...

Michael J. Fox as Marty McFly
Christopher Lloyd as Dr. Emmett "Doc" Brown
Lea Thompson as Lorraine Baines-McFly
Crispin Glover as George McFly
Thomas F. Wilson as Biff Tannen
Claudia Wells as Jennifer Parker
James Tolkan as Mr. Strickland
Marc McClure as Dave McFly
Wendie Jo Sperber as Linda McFly

Plot

Teenager Marty McFly is an aspiring musician dating girlfriend Jennifer Parker in Hill Valley, California. His father George is bullied by his supervisor, Biff Tannen, while his mother Lorraine is an overweight, depressed alcoholic. While dissatisfied with Marty's relationship with Jennifer, Lorraine recalls how she met George when her father hit him with a car.

On October 26, 1985, Marty meets his scientist friend, Dr. Emmett Brown, at a shopping mall parking lot. Doc unveils a time machine built from a modified DeLorean and powered by plutonium stolen from Libyan terrorists. Doc demonstrates the navigation system with the example date of November 5, 1955: the day he conceived the machine. A moment later, the Libyans arrive and shoot him, apparently killing him. Marty escapes in the DeLorean, but inadvertently activates the time machine, and arrives in 1955 without the required plutonium needed to return.

There, Marty encounters the teenage George, who is bullied by classmate Biff. After Marty saves George from an oncoming car and is knocked unconscious, he awakens to find himself tended by an infatuated Lorraine. Marty leaves and tracks down Doc's younger self to help him return to 1985. With no plutonium, Doc explains that the only power source capable of generating the necessary 1.21 gigawatts of electrical power for the time machine is a bolt of lightning. Marty shows Doc a flyer from the future that recounts a lightning strike at the town's courthouse the coming Saturday night. Doc instructs Marty to not leave his house or interact with anyone, as he could inadvertently change the course of history and alter the future; because of this, Doc refuses to heed warnings from Marty about his death in 1985. Marty realizes that he has prevented his parents from meeting and Doc warns Marty that he will be erased from existence if he does not find a way to introduce George to Lorraine. Doc formulates a plan to harness the power of the lightning while Marty sets about introducing his parents, but he antagonizes Biff and his gang in the process.

When Lorraine asks Marty to the upcoming school dance, Marty plans to have George "rescue" Lorraine from Marty's inappropriate advances. The plan goes awry when a drunken Biff attempts to force himself on Lorraine. George arrives to rescue her from Marty, but finds Biff instead. George knocks out Biff and Lorraine follows George to the dance floor, where they kiss and fall in love while Marty plays music with the band. Satisfied that he has secured his future existence, Marty leaves to meet Doc.

As the storm arrives, Marty returns to the clock tower and the lightning strikes on cue, sending Marty back to October 1985. He finds that Doc is not dead, as he had listened to Marty's warnings and worn a bullet-proof vest. Doc takes Marty home, then departs to 2015.

Marty awakens the next morning to find his family changed: George is a self-confident, successful author, Lorraine is physically fit and happy, his brother David is a successful businessman, his sister Linda works in a boutique and has many "boyfriends" and Biff is now an obsequious auto valet. As Marty reunites with Jennifer, the DeLorean appears with Doc, dressed in a futuristic outfit, insisting they accompany him to 2015 to fix a problem with their future children. The trio get inside the DeLorean and disappear into the future.

► Director: Robert Zemeckis
► Writers: Robert Zemeckis, Bob Gale

video_title: Dr. Seuss: Horton Hears A Who! (everyone deserves respect & protection) Kids Picture Book Read Aloud
description:
Dr. Seuss’s “Horton Hears a Who!” is a delightful children’s book written and illustrated by Theodor Seuss Geisel, better known as Dr. Seuss. It was first published in 1954 by Random House. Let me share the enchanting tale of Horton the Elephant and his extraordinary adventure in saving Whoville, a tiny planet perched on a speck of dust.

🐘 Plot Summary:

On the 15th of May, in the Jungle of Nool, Horton, while splashing in a pool, hears a speck of dust talking to him.
Horton realizes that a small person lives on the speck and places it on the top of a red clover, vowing to protect it.
To his surprise, the speck is actually a tiny planet called Whoville, inhabited by microscopic creatures known as Whos.
The Mayor of Whoville implores Horton to safeguard them from harm, and our compassionate elephant hero happily agrees.
Throughout the book, Horton repeats the powerful mantra: “A person’s a person, no matter how small.”
🌟 Key Themes:

The central theme of the book revolves around the idea that every individual, no matter how insignificant, deserves respect and protection.
Horton endures ridicule and harassment from other animals as he strives to care for and ensure the safety of the Whos.
🎥 Adaptations:

“Horton Hears a Who!” has been adapted into a 1970 television special and a 2008 animated film by Blue Sky Studios and 20th Century Fox Animation.
The Broadway musical production “Seussical” also incorporates much of the book’s plot.
Remember, as Dr. Seuss wisely said, “A person’s a person, no matter how small.” 🌱🌏

video_title: Halloween Related Story Books for Kids #toddlers #kindergarten #educational #school #library #kids
description:
Fun Halloween Traditions
1. Costumes! 🎭
This is one of the best parts! On Halloween, kids and adults get to dress up as anything they want. You can be a superhero, a princess, a monster, a character from your favorite movie, or even a funny food item! Long ago, people wore costumes to hide from ghosts. Now, we wear them for fun!

2. Trick-or-Treating 🍬
When it gets dark on Halloween night, kids go out with their friends and family, carrying a bag or a bucket. They walk from house to house, ring the doorbell, and shout "Trick or Treat!"

"Treat" means the person at the door gives you candy or other goodies.

"Trick" is a silly, playful threat to play a trick on them if they don't give a treat (but no one really plays tricks!).

Safety Tip: Always go with a grown-up, and only visit houses with their porch lights on.

3. Pumpkin Carving (Jack-o'-Lanterns) 🎃
People buy pumpkins, scoop out the slimy insides and seeds (you can roast the seeds for a tasty snack!), and carve a funny or scary face into the side. Then, they put a candle or light inside to make it glow!

4. Spooky Decorations 🕸️
You'll see houses and yards decorated with all sorts of spooky things like:

Fake spider webs and giant spiders

Skeletons and ghosts

Gravestones and witches

Bats and black cats

It’s all meant to be fun and a little bit scary, but not too scary!

5. Halloween Parties & Games
Many schools and families have Halloween parties! You might play games like:

Bobbing for Apples: Trying to grab an apple from a tub of water using only your teeth!

Pin the Bow Tie on the Skeleton

Halloween-themed crafts like making ghost lollipops or paper plate masks.

Fun Halloween Symbols & Creatures
You'll see these everywhere in October! They are the classic characters of Halloween.

Ghosts: Friendly (or sometimes shy) spirits.

Witches: Often shown flying on broomsticks with a black cat as a friend.

Black Cats: They're not bad luck on Halloween—they're just a cool, furry friend for witches!

Bats: These nocturnal animals come out at night, just like trick-or-treaters!

Spiders & Webs: They add a creepy-crawly feeling to decorations.

Skeletons: The bony framework inside all of us, but on Halloween, they like to dance!

Yummy Halloween Treats
Halloween isn't just about the candy from trick-or-treating! People make fun Halloween-themed snacks, like:

Caramel Apples: Apples on a stick, covered in sweet, sticky caramel.

Popcorn Balls: Popcorn stuck together in a yummy ball.

"Witch's Fingers": Breadsticks or cookies shaped like creepy fingers.

"Eyeballs": Peeled grapes that feel slimy and look just like eyeballs!

"Punch": A spooky-looking drink, often green or red with gummy worms floating in it.

Safety Tips for a Super Halloween
Be Seen: Wear bright costumes or put reflective tape on your bag and costume so cars can see you.

See Clearly: Make sure your mask doesn't block your vision. It's even better to use face paint instead!

Go with a Grown-Up: Never trick-or-treat alone. Always have a parent or another trusted adult with you.

Check Your Candy: Before you eat ANY candy, let a grown-up look at it first. They'll make sure everything is safe and sealed.

Be Polite: Remember to say "Thank you!" after you get a treat.

Have a Spook-tacular Halloween!
Halloween is a magical night where you can be anyone or anything you want, spend time with friends and family, and collect a bag full of delicious treats. So get creative, be safe, and have a fang-tastic time

video_title: Love, Ruby Valentine (Friendship & Thoughtfulness) #educational #toddlers #kindergarten #kidsbooks
description:
Love, Ruby Valentine, which is actually a beloved existing title by Laurie Friedman.

Summary
Ruby Valentine is a little girl who lives in a heart-shaped house in a town called Loveland with her best friend, a talking parrot named Lovebird. Ruby adores Valentine's Day more than any other day. She loves the crafts, the cards, the sweets, and most of all, she loves telling everyone how much she cares about them.

There's just one problem: In her frantic, excited preparation for the big day—baking treats, writing poems, decorating cards—Ruby works herself into such a tizzy that she sleeps right through Valentine's Day!

She wakes up the day after, February 15th, utterly devastated. All her carefully made cards and treats are still unsent. But with the help of Lovebird, Ruby has a brilliant idea: Just because the calendar says the holiday is over, doesn't mean the love has to be! She decides to deliver her valentines anyway.

To her delight, her friends in Loveland are overjoyed. They love the surprise and agree that spreading love shouldn't be confined to just one day. Ruby learns that the spirit of Valentine's Day—showing appreciation for others—is something you can celebrate any day of the year.

Review and Themes
Love, Ruby Valentine is a charming and heartwarming story that stands out in the genre of holiday books for its gentle and important message.

Key Themes:

The True Meaning of Love & Holidays: The book beautifully argues that the point of a holiday like Valentine's Day isn't the date itself, but the feeling behind it: showing kindness and appreciation for the people in your life.

It's Never Too Late to Show You Care: This is a powerful and comforting message for children (and adults!). A missed deadline doesn't have to mean a missed opportunity for connection.

Friendship and Thoughtfulness: Ruby's motivation is purely out of love for her friends. Her actions are selfless and focused on making others happy.

Problem-Solving: Instead of giving up when she misses the holiday, Ruby thinks creatively and finds a wonderful solution.

Why Kids Love It:

The character of Ruby is relatable—her excitement is contagious and her mistake (oversleeping) is something every child can understand.

The talking parrot, Lovebird, adds a fun, whimsical element.

The colorful, expressive illustrations (by Lynne Avril) bring the town of Loveland and Ruby's emotions vividly to life.

The rhyming text is catchy and enjoyable to read aloud.

Why Parents/Educators Love It:

It's a perfect tool for discussing the emotional core of holidays beyond the commercial aspects.

It helps alleviate anxiety for kids who might feel they've "missed" a special day or event.

It encourages year-round kindness and card-making!

Overall Rating: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (5/5 Stars). A modern classic for Valentine's Day that promotes a timeless message of love.

video_title: Who framed Roger Rabbit - Read Along Story book - As read by Charles Fleischer - Audio Cassette Tape
description:
Who Framed Roger Rabbit (1988) Read Along book and tape read by Charles Fleischer. A toon hating detective is a cartoon rabbit's only hope to prove his innocence when he is accused of murder.

Cast of the full movie version were...

► Bob Hoskins as Eddie Valiant, an alcoholic private investigator who resents Toons. Executive producer Spielberg's first choice for the role was Harrison Ford, but Ford's price was too high. Bill Murray was also considered for the role; however, due to his method of receiving offers for roles, he missed out. Eddie Murphy reportedly turned down the role and later regretted it.

► Christopher Lloyd as Judge Doom, the cold and power-hungry judge of Toontown District's Superior Court. Lloyd was cast because he previously worked with Zemeckis and Amblin Entertainment in Back to the Future. Lloyd compared his part as Doom to his previous role as the Klingon commander Kruge in Star Trek III: The Search for Spock, both being overly evil characters which he considered being "fun to play". Lloyd avoided blinking his eyes while on camera in order to perfectly portray the character.

► Charles Fleischer as the voice of Roger Rabbit, an A-list Toon working for Maroon Cartoons, who is framed for the murder of Marvin Acme, and requests Eddie's help in proving his innocence. To facilitate Hoskins' performance, Fleischer dressed in a Roger bunny suit and "stood in" behind camera for most scenes.[12] Animation director Williams explained Roger Rabbit was a combination of "Tex Avery's cashew nut-shaped head, the swatch of red hair...like Droopy's, Goofy's overalls, Porky Pig's bow tie, Mickey Mouse's gloves and Bugs Bunny-like cheeks and ears." Fleischer also voices Benny the Cab and two members of Doom's Weasel Gang, Psycho and Greasy. Lou Hirsch, who supplied the voice for Baby Herman, was the original choice for Benny the Cab but was replaced by Fleischer.

► Stubby Kaye as Marvin Acme, the jester-like owner of the Acme Corporation. This was Kaye's last film before his retirement in 1988.

► Joanna Cassidy as Dolores, Eddie's on-off girlfriend who works as a waitress.

► Kathleen Turner provides the uncredited voice of Jessica Rabbit, Roger Rabbit's beautiful and flirtatious Toon wife,[14] She loves Roger because, as she says, "he makes me laugh". Amy Irving supplied the singing voice, while Betsy Brantley served as the stand-in. Alan Tilvern, in his final film role, portrays R. K. Maroon, the short-tempered and manipulative owner of "Maroon Cartoon" studios. Lou Hirsch provides the voice of Baby Herman, a mentally middle-aged smoker baby and co-star in Maroon Cartoons. Williams said Baby Herman was a mixture of "Elmer Fudd and Tweety crashed together".

Director: Robert Zemeckis
Writers: Gary K. Wolf (novel), Jeffrey Price (screenplay)

The way Addy comes to understand how this special medicine works makes for a reassuring tale of consolation and healing.

video_title: 👨🏻‍🎨 I am Leonardo da Vinci | Ordinary People Change the World
description:
I am Leonardo da Vinci by Brad Meltzer, illustrated by Christopher Eliopoulos. Read by Riko.

This friendly, fun biography series focuses on the traits that made our heroes great--the traits that kids can aspire to in order to live heroically themselves. Each book tells the story of an icon in a lively, conversational way that works well for the youngest nonfiction readers and that always includes the hero's childhood influences. At the back are an excellent timeline and photos. This book features Leonardo da Vinci, the Renaissance artist and inventor. He always followed his interests, no matter where they led! His quest to fly led him to study birds' wings and his invention designs were the very earliest sketches of helicopters and other flying machines. Da Vinci's hard work and dedication to his curiosities is why we still remember him today.

description:
From the celebrated team behind Creepy Carrots!, Aaron Reynolds and Caldecott Honor winner Peter Brown, comes a hilarious (and just a little creepy) story of a brave rabbit and a very weird pair of underwear.

video_title: 📚 Kids Book Read Aloud: TOO MUCH GLUE by Jason Lefebvre and Zac Retz
description:
Matty loves glue. At home with Dad, he makes glue glasses, glue mustaches, and glue bouncy balls. But at school, his art teacher warns, “Too much glue never dries.”

One day in art class, Matty decides to make the most fantastic glue project ever, with a super-special ingredient - himself! Ignoring his teacher's warnings, Matty belly-flops onto the glue-covered table, rolls all around in the sequins and glitter, and encounters an unexpected glitch - when he tries to get up, he boings right back into the slippery, sticky mess!

This calls for a dose of imagination and a little help from friends. They try a gigantic tow truck, some yarn lassoes, and dabbing Matty with everything in the nurse's bag - but each wacky attempt only makes things worse! Finally Matty gets an idea from his hyperventilating teacher.

Will it work, or will Matty be a half-boy, half-art project stuck- to-a-table forever?

video_title: Ada Twist, Scientist - An Animated Read Aloud with Moving Pictures! *Includes a Classroom Activity*
description:
Ada Twist’s head is full of questions. Like her classmates Iggy and Rosie (stars of their own New York Times bestselling picture books Iggy Peck, Architect and Rosie Revere, Engineer), Ada has always been endlessly curious. Even when her fact-finding missions and elaborate scientific experiments don’t go as planned, Ada learns the value of thinking through problems and continuing to stay curious.

Ada is an inquisitive second grader who was born to be a scientist. She possesses an unusual desire to question everything she encounters: a tick-tocking clock, a pointy-stemmed rose, the hairs in her dad’s nose, and so much more. Ada’s parents and her teacher, Miss Greer, have their hands full as the Ada’s science experiments wreak day-to-day havoc.

On the first day of spring, Ada notices an unpleasant odor. She sets out to discover what might have caused it. Ada uses the scientific method in developing hypotheses in her smelly pursuit. The little girl demonstrates trial and error, while appreciating her family’s full support. In one experiment, she douses fragrances on her cat and attempts to place the frightened feline in the washing machine.

For any parent who wants STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Math) to be fun, this book is a source of inspiration that will get children excited about science, school, learning, and the value of asking “Why?”

video_title: Bees by Karen Hartley & Chris Macro #education #school #library #toddlers #kindergarten #kidsbooks
description:
Bee is a comprehensive but easy-to-understand introduction to the honeybee. It uses simple language and striking, highly magnified photographs to capture a child's attention and explain key scientific concepts.

The book typically covers the following topics:

What is a Bee?: Introduces the honeybee as an insect, pointing out its main body parts (head, thorax, abdomen, wings, legs, antennae, sting).

The Life Cycle: Explains how a bee grows from an egg to a larva, to a pupa, and finally into an adult bee.

Life in the Hive: Describes the social structure of the hive, including the different roles of the queen bee, worker bees, and drone bees.

What Bees Eat: Discusses how bees collect nectar and pollen from flowers.

How Bees Help Us: Explains the vital process of pollination and how bees make honey.

Fun Facts: Often includes interesting tidbits, like how bees communicate through dance.

Distinctive Features
Macro Photography: The book's most memorable feature is its extreme close-up photographs. The images show the bee in incredible detail—its furry body, compound eyes, tongue, and wings—making the insect seem both fascinating and a little alien to young readers.

Simple Text: The text is written in large, clear font with short sentences and paragraphs, perfect for beginning readers or for reading aloud.

Glossary: It includes a simple glossary that defines key terms like antennae, nectar, pollen, and pollination, helping to build a child's scientific vocabulary.

Index and Questions: Like a true non-fiction book, it often has a basic index and sometimes includes questions to encourage further thinking and discussion.

Reception and Legacy
The "Bug Books" series, including Bee, has been widely used in schools and libraries for decades. It is praised for:

Making science accessible and engaging for young children.

Using high-interest photographs to spark curiosity.

Providing clear, accurate information in an age-appropriate way.

It's a staple in early childhood science education and is often a child's first formal introduction to entomology and the importance of insects in our ecosystem.

In summary, Bee by Karen Hartley and Chris Macro is a foundational non-fiction book that uses stunning photography and simple text to teach young children about the biology and importance of the honeybee. It is a well-regarded title from the popular "Bug Books" series.

video_title: Roses are Pink, Your Feet Really Stink (Forgiveness & Apology) #educational #toddlers #kindergarten
description:
"Roses are Pink, Your Feet Really Stink" is a classic and beloved children's picture book.

Here's a detailed overview:

Roses are Pink, Your Feet Really Stink
Author & Illustrator: Diane deGroat
First Published: 1996

Summary
The story is set in a classroom on Valentine's Day. Gilbert, the young opossum protagonist, is tasked with writing valentine poems for all his classmates. He's excited until he realizes he has to make cards for two classmates:

Margaret: Who once told everyone his secret.

Lewis: Who pulled his tail and laughed at him.

Still hurt and angry, Gilbert decides to get a little revenge. Instead of writing nice poems for them, he writes two mean valentines:

For Lewis, he writes: "Roses are pink, violets are blue, your feet are so smelly, they remind me of a zoo!"

For Margaret, he writes: "Roses are red, violets are pink, your face is so freckled, it looks like it's sprinkled with ink!"

To hide his identity, he signs both cards "from your secret pal."

On Valentine's Day during the class party, chaos erupts. Margaret and Lewis receive the mean cards and are very upset. They quickly figure out that the other must have written the nasty card and begin to argue loudly. The whole party is ruined, and everyone is miserable—including Gilbert, who feels terrible about what he did.

Gilbert is consumed by guilt. He realizes his plan for a small bit of revenge backfired and hurt everyone, including himself. To fix the situation, he musters up his courage, admits it was him, and sincerely apologizes. He then takes the time to write two new, genuine, and kind valentines for Margaret and Lewis.

The story ends happily, with the class party back on track and Gilbert learning an important lesson about forgiveness and honesty.

Key Themes
Revenge & Consequences: The book perfectly illustrates how a small act of meanness intended for revenge can have much larger, unintended consequences.

Guilt and Responsibility: Gilbert's internal struggle with guilt is relatable for children. It shows the emotional weight of doing something wrong.

Forgiveness & Apology: The story emphasizes that it's never too late to say you're sorry and make things right. A sincere apology can heal hurt feelings.

Honesty: The central conflict is resolved through honesty, not through hiding the mistake.

Empathy: The book encourages children to think about how their words and actions make others feel.

Why It's a Beloved Children's Book
Relatable Situation: Almost every child has faced a moment of hurt feelings or the temptation to get even with someone who wronged them.

Perfect for Valentine's Day: It's a staple read-aloud in classrooms and homes around the holiday, but its lessons are valuable year-round.

Humorous & Rhyming: The mean poems are funny (in a way kids understand) and catchy. The rhyming text makes it engaging to read aloud.

Positive Resolution: It provides a clear and positive model for conflict resolution: admit your mistake, apologize, and do better.

Great Illustrations: Diane deGroat's animal characters are expressive and charming, perfectly capturing the emotions of the story.

It's a wonderful book that helps children navigate the complexities of friendship and feelings in a way that is both entertaining and instructive.

But if you cant make it outdoors to get your steps in, this 10 minute low impact home workout combines dynamic exercises that are safe to do multiple times throughout your day to keep your blood pressure in a good place. In this routine we have 10 different exercises performed for one minute sequenced back to back. Once we start there are no programmed breaks, but of course listen to your body and modify as needed to meet yourself where you are at today. The goal is just to get moving to feel better together for 10 minutes total.

Daily exercise not only helps control high blood pressure but it also helps manage your weight, strengthen your heart and reduce stress. Trust me nothing feels better than taking control and seeing your health improve. So join me and keep your blood pressure in check the natural way. Use this workout 2-3 times per day for at least a week. Make sure to monitor your blood pressure numbers and share what positive health effects you experience below in the comments.

description:
#readaloud #interactivelearning #kidsstories 
Welcome to Safety Springs! In this interactive children's book, a curious little squirrel takes young readers on a journey through challenging scenarios where the reader is asked to make very important decisions. Covering themes of road safety, fire safety, stranger danger and more – Danger Buster is here to help. But instead of just telling kids what to do, Danger Buster asks them what they would do, encouraging them to think critically and make smart, safe choices.
Danger Buster is thoughtfully designed for children ages 3–5 and offers more than just a story, it’s a conversation starter. Each scenario dives into a real-world potentially dangerous situation, then pauses to ask the reader what the safest choice would be. It’s a fun and engaging way to build safety awareness and confidence to make safe decisions.
As a parent to two young children, the author was inspired to write Danger Buster to help teach her own kids how to navigate the world more safely. She wanted something more than a safety lecture, a playful and empowering way to teach important life lessons through storytelling, interaction, and imagination.
Whether you're a parent, teacher, or caregiver, this book opens the door to meaningful discussions with children about safety in a way that’s engaging, non-scary, fun and rewarding!

video_title: Giraffes Can't Dance (believing in yourself even when others don't) #toddlers #kindergarten #stories
description:
"Giraffes Can't Dance" is a beloved children's picture book written by Giles Andreae and illustrated by Guy Parker-Rees. It's a classic story about self-confidence, embracing your differences, and finding your own rhythm.

Here's a breakdown of the book:

Summary
The story follows Gerald, a tall, graceful giraffe who desperately wants to join in the annual Jungle Dance. The problem is, everyone knows giraffes can't dance. Gerald's knees are crooked, and his legs are thin—he's clumsy and awkward.

When he nervously steps onto the dance floor for the first time, the other animals cruelly mock him. A hyena laughs at his legs, a warthog snorts, and the lions call him "grandpa." Humiliated, Gerald slinks off the dance floor and leaves the party, convinced he is a failure.

Feeling sad and utterly defeated, he wanders into a clearing under the moonlight. There, a wise and friendly cricket offers him a simple but profound piece of advice: "Sometimes when you're different you just need a different song."

The cricket then begins to play a gentle, soothing tune on his violin—a song inspired by the rustling leaves and the sighing wind. Gerald closes his eyes, sways to the music, and finds his body beginning to move. He discovers that he can dance beautifully when he's listening to the right music for him.

The other animals, who had come to see what was happening, are amazed. They watch in awe as Gerald performs a graceful, elegant dance. They cheer for him and declare him the best dancer they've ever seen. From that day on, Gerald proudly dances to his own tune.

Key Themes
Self-Acceptance and Confidence: The core message is about believing in yourself even when others don't.

Embracing Differences: What makes you different is what makes you special. You don't have to conform to others' expectations or abilities.

Kindness vs. Bullying: The story shows the hurtful impact of mocking others and the positive impact of encouragement (from the cricket).

Finding Your Passion: Everyone has their own unique "song" or talent; you just have to find it.

Why It's So Popular
Relatable Message: The feeling of being left out or not being good enough is universal for both children and adults.

Uplifting Story Arc: It moves from sadness and rejection to triumph and joy, which is very satisfying.

Rhyming Text: Giles Andreae's text is written in a catchy, rhythmic rhyme that is incredibly fun to read aloud.

Vibrant Illustrations: Guy Parker-Rees's artwork is bold, colorful, and full of expressive animal characters that leap off the page. The image of Gerald dancing gracefully under the moon is iconic.

In essence, Giraffes Can't Dance is a powerful and joyful reminder that "We can all dance when we find music that we love." It's a staple on children's bookshelves for its positive and empowering message.

description:

A long time ago in China there was a boy named Ping who loved flowers. Anything he planted burst into bloom.

Ping plants his seed and tends it every day. But month after month passes, and nothing grows. When spring comes, Ping must go to the Emperor with nothing but an empty pot.

video_title: George E  Allen Documentary • Northeast Regional Library & George E. Allen Library
description:
George E. Allen was a political strategist and friend to such historical figures as J. Edgar Hoover, Dwight D. Eisenhower, Franklin D. Roosevelt, Harry Truman, Richard Nixon, and others.  In 1973, upon his death, he left the city of Booneville funds to construct a new, larger library building.  The new library opened in 1976 at its current location on W. Church Street.

Allen also left the contents of his home office to be distributed between the Eisenhower Presidential Library and the George E. Allen library.  The collection consists of documents, newspaper clippings, photographs, and paper ephemera, as well as personal artifacts, such as golf balls, engraved lighters, key chains, and VIP/press badges to various events.

In early 2021, former Booneville resident Ted Rubenstein donated funds to be used to preserve and protect the collection.  In the years since, experts from the Mississippi Political Collections at the Mississippi State University Libraries and a professional museum consultant have viewed the items ang given various suggestions for how to archive the collection, as well as how to bring Allen’s political work to a greater audience.

In late 2021 and early 2022, additional large donations by former Booneville residents Steve and Kaye Franks and the H. T. White Family Fund of the Community Foundation for Mississippi were received in support of the project.  In 2023, the Prentiss County Board of Supervisors also contributed funds to go towards the project.

So far, donated funds have been used to purchase locks for the existing glass cases, various sizes of archival boxes, acid-free tissue paper and envelopes, a 10-drawer archival flat file cabinet to replace a damaged flat case, and the informational video above.

Staff at the George E. Allen Library are currently at work sorting items in the collection and placing them in archival grade containers to create an extensive inventory of the collection.   Local Allen expert Marshall Dickerson, along with the Booneville Main Street Association and the Prentiss County Genealogy Society, are working towards bringing attention to Allen’s work through the informational video and a historical marker that will be placed in front of the library in mid-2024.
As funds allow, future plans include placing UV light filters in the Allen room, updating the framed art pieces to be archival grade, printing informational pamphlets about the collection, and creating a tabletop board game based on the historical events surrounding Allen’s life.
A Re-Opening Ceremony is tentatively planned for early – mid 2025.  The ceremony will also include a presentation about the historical significance of Allen’s political career and his close friendships with President Dwight D. Eisenhower.
For more information about the project, contact the George E. Allen Library at 662-728-6553 or the Northeast Regional Library at 662-287-7311.

video_title: The Polar Express - Classic Christmas Holidays #kids #story #books #reading #readaloud #northpole
description:
“The Polar Express” is a timeless fantasy children’s picture book written and illustrated by American author Chris Van Allsburg. First published in 1985, it has become a beloved classic Christmas story for young children 12. Let’s embark on a magical journey aboard the Polar Express:
Plot Summary:
On Christmas Eve, a young boy lies in bed, eagerly listening for the sound of Santa’s sleigh. Instead, he hears the distant chugging of a train—the Polar Express—right outside his window.
The conductor invites him aboard the train, which is filled with other children in their pajamas. They sing carols, enjoy candies and hot chocolate, and race northward through snowy landscapes.
The destination? The North Pole, where Santa Claus will choose one child to receive the first gift of Christmas.
The boy is selected by Santa himself. When asked what he wants, he requests a bell from Santa’s sleigh.
Santa grants his wish, and the boy receives the bell. But as he returns home, he discovers that the bell has fallen through a hole in his pocket.
On Christmas morning, the boy finds the bell under the tree, along with a note from Santa. The bell only rings for those who truly believe.
Fun Facts:
The book’s detailed illustrations and serene storyline earned Chris Van Allsburg the Caldecott Medal for illustration in 1986.
The setting is partially inspired by the author’s hometown of Grand Rapids, Michigan, where he recalls visiting department stores during his childhood 1.(wiki)
“The Polar Express” was adapted into an Oscar-nominated motion-capture film in 2004, starring Tom Hanks and directed by Robert Zemeckis. Van Allsburg served as an executive producer for the film 1.(wiki)
Whether you read it aloud or listen to its enchanting tale, “The Polar Express” reminds us that the magic of Christmas lies in believing. 🚂🎄(AI generated description)

video_title: The Very Hungry Caterpillar (perfect blend of art, education & storytelling) #toddlers #kindergarten
description:
The Very Hungry Caterpillar is a beloved classic of children's literature. Here's a comprehensive overview of the book.

Summary
The story follows a tiny and very hungry caterpillar from its hatching from an egg to its transformation into a beautiful butterfly.

The Beginning: The caterpillar hatches from a tiny egg on a leaf, glowing in the light of the moon. He is very hungry.

The Eating Frenzy: For the first five days (Monday through Friday), the caterpillar eats through an increasing number of fruits:

Monday: One apple

Tuesday: Two pears

Wednesday: Three plums

Thursday: Four strawberries

Friday: Five oranges

He is still hungry!

Saturday's Feast: On Saturday, he indulges in a vast array of junk food, including one piece of chocolate cake, one ice-cream cone, one pickle, one slice of Swiss cheese, one slice of salami, one lollipop, one piece of cherry pie, one sausage, one cupcake, and one slice of watermelon.

The Stomachache: That night, he gets a terrible stomachache because of all the food he ate.

The Transformation: On Sunday, he eats one nice green leaf, feels much better, and is no longer little or hungry. He is now a "big, fat caterpillar." He builds a cocoon around himself (called a cocoon in the book, though butterflies make a chrysalis; this is a common point of discussion) and stays inside for two weeks.

The Climax: He then nibbles a hole in the cocoon and emerges as a stunning, multi-colored butterfly.

Key Details
Author & Illustrator: Eric Carle

First Published: 1969

Publisher: World Publishing Company

Awards: It has won numerous awards and has been translated into over 60 languages. It sells a copy somewhere in the world every 30 seconds!

Why It's Such a Beloved Classic
Interactive & Engaging: The book is famous for its die-cut pages—the holes the caterpillar "eats" through. Children love to poke their fingers through them, making reading a tactile and interactive experience.

Educational Value: It seamlessly teaches multiple concepts:

Counting: The numbers of fruits increase each day.

The Days of the Week: The story is structured around the weekly cycle.

Healthy Eating (and consequences): The caterpillar gets a stomachache after eating too much junk food.

The Life Cycle of a Butterfly: It introduces metamorphosis (egg - caterpillar - cocoon - butterfly) in a simple, memorable way.

Colors and Foods: The bright illustrations introduce a variety of colors and common foods.

Iconic Artwork: Eric Carle's unique collage technique, using hand-painted papers, is vibrant, textured, and instantly recognizable. The final reveal of the large, beautiful butterfly is always a moment of wonder.

Simple, Repetitive Narrative: The repetitive structure ("But he was still hungry!") is perfect for young readers and listeners, allowing them to anticipate and participate in the story.

description:
Join award-winning author David Bowles to read about a boy’s life on the U.S.-Mexico border, visiting his favorite places on The Other Side with his father, spending time with family and friends, and sharing in the responsibility of community care. Get the book: https://bit.ly/47MSj7k

About MY TWO BORDER TOWNS

Early one Saturday morning, a boy prepares for a trip to The Other Side/El Otro Lado. It’s close–just down the street from his school–and it’s a twin of where he lives. To get there, his father drives their truck along the Rio Grande and over a bridge, where they’re greeted by a giant statue of an eagle. Their outings always include a meal at their favorite restaurant, a visit with Tío Mateo at his jewelry store, a cold treat from the paletero, and a pharmacy pickup. On their final and most important stop, they check in with friends seeking asylum and drop off much-needed supplies.

My Two Border Towns by David Bowles, with stunning watercolor illustrations by Erika Meza, is the loving story of a father and son’s weekend ritual, a demonstration of community care, and a tribute to the fluidity, complexity, and vibrancy of life on the U.S.-Mexico border.

video_title: Worry Thoughts: A Story to Help Children Manage Worries and Anxious Thoughts Read Aloud
description:
Worry Thoughts started out as a rhyming poem that the author wrote for his daughters when they were quite young. It is now an engaging storybook with full-page illustrations that brings the poem to life.

Whether it was reading the poem to them when they were very young, or them reading it to themselves as they got older, the poem helped them reset. Was it the cure-all for all their worries and anxious thoughts, no, not at all, it just became one of many ways that helped them change the relationship they had with their worry thoughts. And that’s what it’s all about.
It teaches yet another coping skill that can help the child feel in control when they have worry thoughts.
It makes for a wonderful storytime book for the parent or teacher to talk about worries and ways to help manage those anxious thoughts.
Also included in the book is a comic strip rendition of the poem as well as the original poem with the hope that the book can always be a go-to for the child as they grow up.

description:
Join us for a magical read-aloud of The Raft, the heartwarming and beautifully crafted picture book written and illustrated by Jim LaMarche. 

Meet Nicky, a city boy who isn’t happy about spending his summer with his artistic grandmother in the Wisconsin woods—with no TV and no city distractions. But everything changes when a mysterious, weathered wooden raft floats down the river and into his life.

As Nicky spends his days drifting down the river, sketching the incredible wildlife, and discovering the hidden magic of the wilderness, he finds a deep connection to nature and a newfound bond with his grandmother. It is a gentle, stunning story that inspires children to slow down, look closer at the world around them, and unlock their own inner artist.

Monster birthday parties are different from the parties that children have and if you want to know just how different they can be, you’ll have to read Monster Grunter’s Birthday Bash to find out.
One thing you can be sure of is that all the monster children will have a good time at Grunter’s party and that they’ll all go home happy and well-fed. But why does he light his candles instead of blowing them out? And what is inside those gift boxes that could be so special?

video_title: 🖍️ The Day the Crayons Quit 😡 Kids Book Short Funny Read Aloud
description:
A boy discovers his workforce of coloring implements has amassed an array of grievances against him!

Mr. Paul reads aloud "The Day the Crayons Quit" by Drew Daywalt, with pictures by Oliver Jeffers. This short, colorful picture book, excellent either for read-aloud time at school or family bedtime at home, uses comedy to introduce several important concepts, like unintended consequences; finding constructive ways—such as a letter—to express one's feelings; and a kid-friendly example of workplace solidarity. This story would be a perfect complement for May Day or Labor Day, and is aimed at students in the primary grades—kindergarten, first grade, and second grade—though it may be enjoyed by children outside of those ages.

It is also a fun and simple way to introduce the literary device of the epistolary story—that is, a story told through letters—which could be followed by a writing exercise in which students create their own such stories.

Mo Willems’ award-winning formula shines through in this 18th installment of the Elephant & Piggie series. The cover alone—a pigeon ornament perched atop their convertible—hints at the whimsy within.

Whether you’re a parent reading aloud or a budding reader exploring speech bubbles, “Let’s Go for a Drive!” promises laughter, surprises, and the joy of friendship. Buckle up and join Elephant and Piggie on their unforgettable adventure!

video_title: The Going to Bed Book (holds toddler's attention) #educational #toddlers #kindergarten #kidsbooks
description:
The Going to Bed Book by Sandra Boynton is a beloved classic children's book. Here's a detailed overview perfect for parents, caregivers, or anyone curious about it.

Overview of The Going to Bed Book
Author & Illustrator: Sandra Boynton
Target Age Range: 0-4 years old
Genre: Board Book, Bedtime Story

This book has been a staple on nursery bookshelves since its publication in 1982. It's known for its charming, silly animals, gentle rhymes, and simple, calming routine that perfectly signals it's time for sleep.

The Story (Plot Summary)
The story follows a group of adorable animals—including a pig, a rabbit, a dog, and a hippo—aboard a whimsical ark as they go through their nightly routine before bed.

The routine is straightforward and relatable for little ones:

The sun is setting over the sea.

The animals go below deck to take a bath in a big tub together.

They hang their towels and find their pajamas.

They brush their teeth (with a moose brushing a tooth that's almost as big as he is!).

They all do some exercises on deck (a famously silly part where they run, bend, and stretch under the moon).

Finally, they turn off the light and all go to sleep as the ark rocks gently under the stars.

The entire process is a calming, step-by-step wind-down that mirrors what parents hope to do with their own children at bedtime.

Why It's So Popular and Effective
Perfect Rhyme and Rhythm: Boynton's rhymes are simple, catchy, and never forced. The rhythmic text is soothing and almost musical when read aloud, which helps lull children to a sleepy state.

Calming Routine: The book acts as a "script" for bedtime. Children love predictability, and reading this book every night creates a powerful signal that the day is ending and sleep is coming.

Gentle Humor: The illustrations are full of sweet and silly details that parents and children love (like the tiny rabbit in the giant bath tub or all the animals in their matching striped pajamas). This makes the reading experience joyful and engaging.

Soothing Artwork: The illustrations are soft, rounded, and friendly. The color palette starts with warm evening hues and gradually shifts to cool, dark night-time blues and purples, visually guiding the child toward sleep.

Durable Format: As a classic board book, it's perfectly sized for small hands and can withstand being chewed on and tossed around by its youngest readers.

Sample Text
A classic passage that demonstrates the rhythm and rhyme:

"The sun has set not long ago.
Now everybody goes below
to take a bath in one big tub
with soap all over—SCRUB SCRUB SCRUB!"

Potential "Silly" Questions from Kids (and How to Answer Them!)
"Why are they on a boat?" It's a magical bedtime ark! It's not meant to be realistic—it's just a fun, cozy place for their routine.

"Why are they exercising before bed?" This is the book's most famous quirk! You can laugh about it together: "Isn't that silly? We get our wiggles out before our bath. They must have a lot of extra energy!"

"Why does the rhinoceros only have one pajama button done?" That’s part of Boynton’s charm! It makes the characters feel more relatable and imperfect.

Overall Verdict
The Going to Bed Book is a perfect first bedtime book. It’s short enough to hold a toddler's attention, rhythmic enough to be soothing, and familiar enough to become a cherished part of the family routine. It’s no wonder it has remained a bestseller for over 40 years.

It's a highly recommended gift for new parents and a must-have for any child's first library.

Common Types of Easter Kids' Books
 The Biblical Story (The Passion Narrative)
These books tell the traditional story from the Bible, from Jesus's entry into Jerusalem to His resurrection. They are carefully tailored for young ears.

Key Elements:

The Joyful Entry: Jesus riding into Jerusalem on a donkey while people wave palm branches.

The Last Supper: Often simplified as a special meal with his friends.

video_title: Dia De Los Muertos Books Collection | Kids & Family Together Picture Story | Read Aloud- English
description:
Dia de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, is a traditional Mexican holiday celebrated from October 31 to November 2 each year. It’s a time when families welcome back the souls of their deceased relatives for a brief reunion that includes food, drink, and celebration. The holiday is a blend of Mesoamerican ritual, European religion, and Spanish culture.

The roots of the Day of the Dead go back some 3,000 years, to the rituals honoring the dead in pre-Columbian Mesoamerica. The Aztecs and other Nahua people living in what is now central Mexico held a cyclical view of the universe and saw death as an integral, ever-present part of life.

Upon dying, a person was believed to travel to Chicunamictlán, the Land of the Dead. Only after getting through nine challenging levels, a journey of several years, could the person’s soul finally reach Mictlán, the final resting place.

In Nahua rituals honoring the dead, traditionally held in August, family members provided food, water, and tools to aid the deceased in this difficult journey. This inspired the contemporary Day of the Dead practice in which people leave food or other offerings on their loved ones’ graves, or set them out on makeshift altars called ofrendas in their homes.

The Day of the Dead is not a Mexican version of Halloween, though the two holidays do share some traditions, including costumes and parades. On the Day of the Dead, it’s believed that the border between the spirit world and the real world dissolves.

The multi-day holiday involves family and friends gathering to pay respects and to remember friends and family members who have died. These celebrations can take a humorous tone, as celebrants remember funny events and anecdotes about the departed. Traditions connected with the holiday include honoring the deceased using calaveras and marigold flowers known as cempazúchitl, building home altars called ofrendas with the favorite foods and beverages of the departed, and visiting graves with these items as gifts for the deceased.

The celebration is not solely focused on the dead, as it is also common to give gifts to friends such as candy sugar skulls, to share traditional pan de muerto with family and friends, and to write light-hearted and often irreverent verses in the form of mock epitaphs dedicated to living friends and acquaintances, a literary form known as calaveras literarias.

In 2008, the tradition was inscribed in the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity by UNESCO. (AI generated).

description:
"Bedtime With Blippi" is a colorful, hardcover picture book designed for toddlers and preschoolers. It takes the familiar, excitable character of Blippi and places him in a soothing, bedtime routine context, making it an excellent transition from playtime to sleep for young fans.

Key Details
Author: Based on the character created by Stevin John. Often published under the name "Blippi" or as part of the "Blippi" brand.

Illustrator: The book features the classic, bright 3D-style artwork that matches the Blippi YouTube videos and live-action show.

Target Age Range: 1-4 years old.

Format: Typically a sturdy board book or hardcover, perfect for little hands.

Plot Summary
The story follows Blippi as he goes through his own bedtime routine, showing young readers that even their favorite explorer needs to wind down and get ready for sleep.

Winding Down: The book starts with Blippi finishing up his day of play and learning. He might put away his toys (like his orange and blue helicopter) and change out of his signature outfit.

The Routine: Blippi goes through all the familiar steps of a bedtime routine, which mirrors what parents do with their own children:

Taking a warm, bubbly bath.

Brushing his teeth.

Putting on his pajamas.

Reading a bedtime story.

Saying Goodnight: Blippi says goodnight to all the things he loves, like his friends (often his puppy and other animals), his toys, and the moon outside his window.

Sweet Dreams: The book ends with Blippi cozy in bed, ready for sleep, encouraging the child reader to do the same.

Themes and Educational Value
Routine Reinforcement: This is the book's strongest feature. It helps normalize and teach the importance of a consistent bedtime routine, making real-life bedtime easier.

Early Learning Concepts: Like all Blippi content, the book incorporates basic learning:

Colors: Identifying the colors of objects (orange helicopter, blue pajamas, etc.).

Objects/Nouns: Labeling everyday items like toothbrush, toothpaste, bath toys, and pillow.

Sequencing: Understanding the order of events (first we take a bath, then we brush our teeth).

Social-Emotional Learning: It models self-care and healthy habits in a fun, engaging way.

What Parents and Kids Love About It
Familiar Character: For children who are already fans of the Blippi videos, this book is an instant hit. It feels like a special appearance from a beloved friend.

Calming Influence: It successfully takes Blippi's typically high-energy persona and channels it into a calm, quiet narrative, which helps signal to kids that it's time to sleep.

Interactive and Engaging: The bright, bold illustrations keep children engaged. Parents can ask questions like, "Can you find Blippi's toothbrush?" or "What color are his pajamas?"

Durable: The board book format can withstand being handled by toddlers.

Potential Considerations
Character Voice: If you read it aloud, you might feel pressured to do the distinctive "Blippi voice." (This is optional, of course, but kids might love it!).

Simple Plot: The story is very straightforward—it's a routine, not a complex narrative. This is perfect for the target age group but might be too simple for older preschoolers.

Final Verdict
"Bedtime With Blippi" is a highly effective and enjoyable bedtime book for toddlers. It successfully leverages a popular character to promote positive habits and provide a comforting, predictable read before sleep. It's a great tool for parents looking to make the bedtime process smoother and more fun.

description:

Read by Sandy Donahue, Booneville Librarian

New York Times bestselling duo Doreen Cronin and Betsy Lewin’s beloved story about Little Duck’s birthday is now available as a Level 2 Ready-to-Read!

Happy first birthday, Little Duck!

Everyone wants to look their best for the party. But Little Duck has never had a birthday before—so how better to learn how to prepare than to do what all the other animals do! The sheep trim their wool—so Little Duck trims her feathers. The pigs need a mud bath—so Little Duck squishes and squashes, too. All over the barnyard Little Duck snips, slurps, and shimmy shakes herself ready until...WHOOPS! It’s party picture time—and Little Duck is a big mess. No matter—it’s not something Farmer Brown’s frosted maple cake can’t fix!

One day, while walking through the forest, Steve finds a beautiful gold horn. Instantly, he knows he has found the path to being exceptional. (That means special.) Steve ties the horn to the top of his head and prances off to show his friends. Everyone but Bob is impressed—and many are so inspired, they start tying items to the top of their heads as well.

But when Steve finds his horn has gone missing, he’s devastated. (That means really bummed.) Frantically, he searches to find it. Because without his beautiful gold horn, Steve can’t be an exceptional horse. Can he? Come along with Steve as he sets out to find an answer, and a valuable life lesson along the way.

Narrated by the exceptional Rainn Wilson, A Horse Named Steve is a story about how you can be special whether you’re different or whether you’re just like everyone else. It also celebrates the child-like impulse to be and do what feels fun in the moment. With light vocabulary-building elements, A Horse Named Steve is written and illustrated by Kelly Collier, and published by Kids Can Press.

video_title: Our Skin - Kids Read Aloud Audiobook
description:
Based on the research that race, gender, consent, and body positivity should be discussed with toddlers on up, this read-aloud board book series offers adults the opportunity to begin important conversations with young children in an informed, safe, and supported way.
   Developed by experts in the fields of early childhood and activism against injustice, this topic-driven board book offers clear, concrete language and beautiful imagery that young children can grasp and adults can leverage for further discussion.
   While young children are avid observers and questioners of their world, adults often shut down or postpone conversations on complicated topics because it's hard to know where to begin. Research shows that talking about issues like race and gender from the age of two not only helps children understand what they see, but also increases self-awareness, self-esteem, and allows them to recognize and confront things that are unfair, like discrimination and prejudice.
   This first book in the series begins the conversation on race, with a supportive approach that considers both the child and the adult. Stunning art accompanies the simple and interactive text, and the backmatter offers additional resources and ideas for extending this discussion.

video_title: Green Eggs and Ham by Dr. Seuss | Kids & Family Picture Story Book | Read Aloud-American English |
description:
“Green Eggs and Ham” is a delightful children’s book by Dr. Seuss, first published on August 12, 1960. This whimsical tale has captured the hearts of readers young and old. Let’s explore the colorful world of Sam-I-Am and his persistent quest to share a peculiar dish:

Plot Summary:
Sam-I-Am enthusiastically offers a man a plate of green eggs and ham.
However, the man adamantly declares that he hates this unusual food.
Undeterred, Sam continues to pester him, suggesting various scenarios: eating green eggs and ham in a house, with a mouse, in a boat, with a goat, on a train, in a tree, in the dark, in the rain, and even in a boat!
Each time, the man rebuffs him, refusing to try the dish.
Finally, in a twist of fate, Sam-I-Am tastes the colorful delicacy himself, hoping it will convince the man to give it a chance.
To everyone’s surprise, the man takes a bite and joyfully declares that the dish is quite tasty!
Background:
“Green Eggs and Ham” is part of Seuss’s “Beginner Books” series, intentionally written with very simple vocabulary for beginning readers.
Remarkably, the entire book consists of just 50 words, a challenge Seuss undertook after completing “The Cat in the Hat” using 236 words.
The 50 words include familiar ones like “I,” “you,” “like,” “here,” “they,” “try,” “with,” and “thank.”
It’s a testament to Seuss’s creativity that he wove an engaging story with such a limited vocabulary.
Reception and Cultural Impact:
Since its publication, “Green Eggs and Ham” has become a beloved classic.
By 2001, it was the fourth-best-selling English-language children’s hardcover book.
The National Education Association (NEA) conducted a survey, and children ranked it third among their favorite books, just above another Dr. Seuss classic, “The Cat in the Hat.”
Teachers also consistently rank it highly.
In 2012, Scholastic Parent & Child magazine included it among the “100 Greatest Books for Kids.

Puss in Boots" is a classic fairy tale written by Charles Perrault. First published in 1697, it tells the story of a clever cat who uses his wit and charm to help his poor master rise from rags to riches. This beloved tale has been adapted into various forms of media over the years, including films, plays, and children's books.


The story is set in a small village in France, where a miller passes away and leaves his three sons with his only possession - a mill, a donkey, and a cat named Puss. While the eldest son receives the mill, and the middle son receives the donkey, the youngest son, who is considered the least fortunate, is given the seemingly worthless cat.

Little do they know, Puss is no ordinary cat. He is highly intelligent and resourceful, and he sets out to help his master improve his circumstances. Puss starts by catching rabbits and presenting them to the king as a gift from his "Marquis of Carabas" master. Impressed by the cat's offerings, the king takes notice of the Marquis of Carabas and invites him to his palace.

Puss then devises a plan to make his master appear wealthy and influential. He instructs him to bathe in a river, while he hides his clothes. As the king's carriage approaches, Puss tells the king that his master has been robbed while swimming and that the thieves took his clothes. The king, believing the story, offers the Marquis of Carabas new clothes from his own wardrobe.

As the cat and his master continue on their journey, Puss encounters a castle inhabited by a powerful ogre. Puss cleverly tricks the ogre into transforming into a mouse, and he swiftly catches and devours him. With the castle now belonging to his master, Puss invites the king and princess to visit, impressing them with the grandeur of the estate.

In the end, the king is so taken by the Marquis of Carabas and the beauty of the princess that he arranges for them to be married, thus elevating the miller's son from poverty to nobility. Puss, having completed his mission, is rewarded with a life of luxury, becoming a pampered pet in the castle.

video_title: Learn All About Sharks #kids #story #books #reading #learning #readaloud #shark #water #ocean
description:
Sharks are fascinating creatures that have roamed the oceans for over 400 million years, even before dinosaurs existed. Here are some interesting facts about them:

Characteristics
Skeleton: Unlike most fish, sharks have a skeleton made of cartilage, which is lighter and more flexible than bone.
Body Shape: Their fusiform (rounded and tapering at both ends) body shape helps reduce drag and requires minimal energy to swim.
Teeth: Sharks have several rows of teeth that are constantly replaced throughout their lives.
Diversity
There are over 500 species of sharks, ranging from the tiny dwarf lantern shark, which is only about 8 inches long, to the massive whale shark, which can grow up to 40 feet. Some well-known species include:

Great White Shark: Known for its size and power.
Hammerhead Shark: Recognizable by its unique head shape.
Whale Shark: The largest shark, which feeds on plankton.
Unique Abilities
Electroreception: Sharks have special organs called ampullae of Lorenzini that allow them to detect electrical fields produced by other animals.
Tapetum Lucidum: This layer in their eyes helps them see better in low light conditions.
Conservation
Many shark species are threatened due to overfishing and the shark fin trade. Conservation efforts are crucial to protect these important predators and maintain the balance of marine ecosystems.

In 2000, Maria Rivas immigrated from El Salvador to the United States. A year later, she received Temporary Protected Status (TPS) to stay and work legally in the U.S.
